articles.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
articles.body:
We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”
“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”
Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.
Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days.
Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.
But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down
Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.
And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.
Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.
But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.
So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.
Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.
Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.
And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.
But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.
Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.
I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.
I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.
Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.
Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.
Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.
People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.
Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?
Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

articles.title: Should Jensen Huang Return as Nvidia's CEO? Supporters and Critics Disagree
articles.body:
Should Jensen Huang Return as Nvidia's CEO? Supporters and Critics Disagree (theverge.com) 1
			
		 	
				"Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia's chief executive," reports Reuters, "and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter."
One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House...
The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang.  
The Guardian adds that Friday two major Nvidia shareholders "urged the board to keep 'all options' open."
In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look "outside" the company for its next chief. "They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said on Fox News.  Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang's affair with the alleged spy for Beijing... Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang's behaviour within the next 10 days.   
The Guardian also notes Elon Musk "and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company... "
The letter demands that the company's board members "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts"...  Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang's return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco's most renowned business incubator.  Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had "erred, yes — to err is to be human — but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company". More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company's workforce.  
But it's difficult to verify the authenticity of signatories, notes The Verge:
  Business Insider reports that signatures include "Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor" and "Xi Jingping," likely a misspelling of Chinese president Xi Jinping.
Not all believe Jensen Huang should be allowed to return to his seat. According to the Financial Times, one ally acknowledged that, "Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense."  23andMe founder Anne Wojcicki told Bloomberg that "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible ... We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Wojcicki endured a messy public divorce from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, after it was revealed he was having an affair with an employee.

articles.title: Emacs Is My Browser
articles.body:
In my ever-increasing desire to use emacs as my sole computing environment, I have started to take browsing the web inside it far more seriously. Where I previously had thought EWW to be a niceity but far from capable, after using it for a few days it seems to be useable for about 85-90% of use cases - even on the javascript riddled hellhole that is the internet.
Why?#
I have seen in my own use of the modern browser (chromium/firefox) that it is far too easy to get distracted - too easy to get off track and fall down rabbit holes that take over my day. There are infinite suggestions as to how I should spend my time, uncountable shiny objects that take my eye off the prize that is Creativity and Depth. This has been momentously negated with EWW (or any terminal browser, lynx or browsh for the non-emacs users).
In addition to this, my belief is that we should make strides toward leaving behind Layer 8 of the internet - the limiting frontends of social platforms and locked away corners of the net that limit actual discourse (Discord, I’m looking at you). We have given up far too much to big tech platforms, and gotten nothing of value in return, to the point that many now think the internet is dying.
The internet is just a delivery mechanism, and for people that see it for what it really is, the internet has never been more alive. I truly recommend using the internet as if it was 1999.
Even on my phone, I’ve stopped using javascript frontends and embraced using eww in emacs (in termux), only falling back to fennec for about 5-10% of usecases:
I find this way of using the internet far higher in signal than any other method, allowing me to look up information, read documentation, and produce more.
How I am doing this#
For the uninitiated, emacs ships with EWW (Emacs Web Wowser) permitting you to browse the web with image and gif (when did gifs die, I almost never see them these days!) support directly inside Emacs.
I have some sane defaults that permit ease of use such as using B for back, U for yanking url at point, and a few built in functions.
Hitting R will invoke eww readable which is similar to reader mode in firefox, removing headers and footers and focusing in on the text on page.  Useful.
You can send the page to your default browser with &. If a page doesn’t render nicely, this is a good fallback.
D will download images locally, b goes back a page, a will save bookmarks. All of this makes browsing in eww truly enjoyable.
I have also set .pdf to open in emacs, .mp4 and youtube/video hosting links to open in mpv, and gopher/gemini links to open in elpher. Elpher is the EWW for the gopher and gemini protocols, the smolweb that is all signal and no noise.
EWW uses Shr to render html, so you will see some callouts to that in my configuration below:
My browser.el setup:#
Here’s how I have configured EWW to work in my Emacs configuration:
My default search engine is my own Searx instance, a privacy respecting frontend that amalgamates all other search engines.
Limitations#
You will not be watching youtube videos or reading Tweets (x.com is adversarial to non-JS supported browsers). You will not be using social media, nor will you be logging into any platforms. You will not be doing your online banking, filling in government forms, or viewing client portals.
The usecase is quick web searches, documentation, and reading blogs generally.  Once more, hitting & in any web page will bring up your default browser to continue your session in chromium or firefox when you do run into pages that don’t work well in EWW.
Conclusion#
I have reverted all my url functions to default to browsing in EWW, so any web interaction must first go through EWW. This has encouraged me to deeply consider what I am doing online first and foremost, and then only falling back to a modern browser when needed. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much I am able to do inside emacs, and continue to move toward using it as my computing environment in perpetuity.
As always, God bless, and until next time.
If you enjoyed this post, consider Supporting my work, Checking out my book, Working with me, or sending me an Email to tell me what you think.

I have seen in my own use of the modern browser (chromium/firefox) that it is far too easy to get distracted - too easy to get off track and fall down rabbit holes that take over my day. There are infinite suggestions as to how I should spend my time, uncountable shiny objects that take my eye off the prize that is Creativity and Depth. This has been momentously negated with EWW (or any terminal browser, lynx or browsh for the non-emacs users).
In addition to this, my belief is that we should make strides toward leaving behind Layer 8 of the internet - the limiting frontends of social platforms and locked away corners of the net that limit actual discourse (Discord, I’m looking at you). We have given up far too much to big tech platforms, and gotten nothing of value in return, to the point that many now think the internet is dying.
The internet is just a delivery mechanism, and for people that see it for what it really is, the internet has never been more alive. I truly recommend using the internet as if it was 1999.
Even on my phone, I’ve stopped using javascript frontends and embraced using eww in emacs (in termux), only falling back to fennec for about 5-10% of usecases:
I find this way of using the internet far higher in signal than any other method, allowing me to look up information, read documentation, and produce more.
How I am doing this#
For the uninitiated, emacs ships with EWW (Emacs Web Wowser) permitting you to browse the web with image and gif (when did gifs die, I almost never see them these days!) support directly inside Emacs.
I have some sane defaults that permit ease of use such as using B for back, U for yanking url at point, and a few built in functions.
Hitting R will invoke eww readable which is similar to reader mode in firefox, removing headers and footers and focusing in on the text on page.  Useful.
You can send the page to your default browser with &. If a page doesn’t render nicely, this is a good fallback.
D will download images locally, b goes back a page, a will save bookmarks. All of this makes browsing in eww truly enjoyable.
I have also set .pdf to open in emacs, .mp4 and youtube/video hosting links to open in mpv, and gopher/gemini links to open in elpher. Elpher is the EWW for the gopher and gemini protocols, the smolweb that is all signal and no noise.
EWW uses Shr to render html, so you will see some callouts to that in my configuration below:
My browser.el setup:#
Here’s how I have configured EWW to work in my Emacs configuration:
My default search engine is my own Searx instance, a privacy respecting frontend that amalgamates all other search engines.
Limitations#
You will not be watching youtube videos or reading Tweets (x.com is adversarial to non-JS supported browsers). You will not be using social media, nor will you be logging into any platforms. You will not be doing your online banking, filling in government forms, or viewing client portals.
The usecase is quick web searches, documentation, and reading blogs generally.  Once more, hitting & in any web page will bring up your default browser to continue your session in chromium or firefox when you do run into pages that don’t work well in EWW.
Conclusion#
I have reverted all my url functions to default to browsing in EWW, so any web interaction must first go through EWW. This has encouraged me to deeply consider what I am doing online first and foremost, and then only falling back to a modern browser when needed. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much I am able to do inside emacs, and continue to move toward using it as my computing environment in perpetuity.
As always, God bless, and until next time.
If you enjoyed this post, consider Supporting my work, Checking out my book, Working with me, or sending me an Email to tell me what you think.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 483 (I'm Not a Freezer)
    
draft-banffy-httpbis-not-a-freezer-00

Independent Submission                                         R. Bánffy
Internet-Draft                                          15 November 2026
Intended status: Informational                                          
Expires: 19 May 2027
  The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 483 (I'm Not a Freezer)
                 draft-banffy-httpbis-not-a-freezer-00
Abstract
   This document defines the Hypertext Transfer Protocol status code 483
   (I'm Not a Freezer).  A server returns this status code when it
   understands a request that requires freezing or refrigeration
   capabilities but is not capable of providing those capabilities.
   This document also clarifies the distinction between a freezer, a
   refrigerator, a server operating at a low temperature, a frozen
   software process, and an online service advertising "cold storage".
Status of This Memo
   This Internet-Draft is submitted in full conformance with the
   provisions of BCP 78 and BCP 79.
   Internet-Drafts are working documents of the Internet Engineering
   Task Force (IETF).  Note that other groups may also distribute
   working documents as Internet-Drafts.  The list of current Internet-
   Drafts is at https://datatracker.ietf.org/drafts/current/.

   and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any

   Provisions Relating to IETF Documents (https://trustee.ietf.org/

   Please review these documents carefully, as they describe your rights
   and restrictions with respect to this document.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 1]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
Table of Contents
   1.  Introduction  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   2
   2.  Conventions and Definitions . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   2
   3.  The 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) Status Code . . . . . . . . . . .   3
   4.  Client Behavior . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   4
   5.  Applicability . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   4
   6.  Example: Electronic Mail Concerning Frozen Goods  . . . . . .   5
   7.  Relationship to Status Code 418 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   6
   8.  Distinguishing Refrigerators from Freezers  . . . . . . . . .   7
   9.  Intermediaries and Cold-Chain Proxies . . . . . . . . . . . .   7
   10. Caching Considerations  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   7
   11. Security Considerations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   8
   12. Privacy Considerations  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   8
   13. IANA Considerations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   9
   14. Implementation Considerations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   9
   15. Acknowledgments . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   9
   16. Normative References  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  10
   17. Informative References  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  10
   Author's Address  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  10
1.  Introduction
   HTTP status codes communicate the result of attempting to understand
   and satisfy a request.  Existing status codes cover malformed
   requests, missing resources, unsupported media types, and servers
   that are temporarily unavailable.
   No registered status code clearly indicates that a server understood
   a request but cannot satisfy it because the request requires the
   server to be a freezer.
   This ambiguity can cause clients to repeat requests, select
   inappropriate fallback services, place perishable goods near
   computing equipment, or otherwise confuse information technology
   infrastructure with domestic or industrial refrigeration equipment.
   This document addresses that ambiguity by defining the 483 (I'm Not a
   Freezer) status code.
2.  Conventions and Definitions
   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
   "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and
   "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP
   14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all
   capitals, as shown here.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 2]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   Freezer
      An apparatus capable of maintaining its contents at a temperature
      below the freezing point of water for a sustained period.
      Software containers, frozen processes, cold-storage services, and
      servers located in cold climates are not necessarily freezers.
   Refrigerator
      An apparatus that maintains contents below ambient temperature but
      does not necessarily maintain them below the freezing point of
      water.
   Cold storage
      A term that might refer to refrigerated physical storage,
      infrequently accessed data storage, an offline cryptographic
      wallet, or other facilities that are insufficiently warm.  Use of
      the term does not establish freezer capability.
   Freezer-capable server
      An HTTP server associated with equipment that can perform the
      freezing operation requested by the client.  Merely operating
      inside a freezer does not necessarily make an HTTP server freezer-
      capable.
3.  The 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) Status Code
   This document extends the HTTP status-code semantics defined in
   [HTTP] with the 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) status code.  The status code
   indicates that the server understood the request but cannot satisfy
   it because the requested operation requires freezing or refrigeration
   capabilities that the server does not possess.
   A server MAY return 483 when all of the following conditions apply:
   *  The request can be parsed and understood.
   *  Satisfying the request would require the server to freeze,
      refrigerate, chill, or preserve a physical item by reducing its
      temperature.
   *  The server is not capable of performing the requested temperature-
      control operation.
   A server MUST NOT return 483 merely because:
   *  its operating temperature is below ambient temperature;
   *  it uses liquid, air, immersion, or phase-change cooling;
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 3]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   *  it provides a service described as "cold storage";
   *  one or more software processes have been frozen;
   *  its physical location is cold;
   *  its hostname contains words such as "freezer", "ice", "arctic",
      "frost", or "cold"; or
   *  it is unresponsive in a way informally described as "frozen".
   A 483 response SHOULD contain a representation explaining that the
   selected server lacks the required refrigeration capability.  Where
   appropriate, the representation MAY identify a freezer-capable
   alternative.
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: text/plain
   This server is not a freezer and cannot satisfy the requested operation.
4.  Client Behavior
   A client receiving a 483 response SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the
   same request to the same server unless it has reason to believe that
   the server has subsequently acquired suitable refrigeration
   capabilities.
   A client MAY attempt the request against another origin if that
   origin is known to be freezer-capable.
   A client MUST NOT interpret a 483 response as evidence that the
   server is a refrigerator.  The response communicates a lack of
   freezer capability and makes no claim concerning lesser, adjacent, or
   unrelated cooling capabilities.
   Clients SHOULD avoid automatically redirecting physical goods based
   solely on URI authority components, DNS names, electronic mail
   addresses, service banners, or unverified appliance metadata.
5.  Applicability
   Status code 483 is applicable when a request crosses a boundary
   between digital instructions and physical temperature-control
   operations.
   Examples include:
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 4]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   *  an HTTP-controlled kitchen appliance receiving a request to freeze
      food;
   *  an industrial control gateway receiving a request to preserve a
      sample below a specified temperature;
   *  a logistics service receiving an instruction that requires a cold-
      chain facility that it does not operate; and
   *  a general-purpose HTTP server receiving a request intended for a
      refrigeration appliance.
   Status code 483 is not intended to report CPU thermal throttling,
   data-center cooling failures, insufficient heat dissipation,
   unresponsive software, immutable data, object freezing in programming
   languages, or process suspension.
6.  Example: Electronic Mail Concerning Frozen Goods
   Consider an HTTP service that accepts electronic mail for delivery to
   suitable appliances.  A client might inadvertently attempt to deliver
   a message intended for a freezer:
   POST /mail HTTP/1.1
   Host: mail.example
   Content-Type: message/rfc822
   From: alice@example.com
   To: freezer@example.com
   Date: Tue, 3 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000
   Message-ID: <peas-483@example.com>
   Subject: Please freeze these peas
   Dear Freezer,
   Please maintain the attached peas at approximately -18 degrees
   Celsius until further notice.
   Regards,
   Alice
   If the selected service is not a freezer and cannot cause the
   requested freezing operation to occur, it MAY reject the request with
   status code 483:
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 5]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: text/plain
   This server is not a freezer and cannot satisfy the requested operation.
   An implementation MUST NOT infer refrigeration capability solely from
   an electronic mail address containing the strings "freezer",
   "refrigerator", "cold", "ice", or similar terminology.
   The recipient address identifies the intended appliance but does not
   prove that the HTTP service handling the message controls that
   appliance.
   The domain names and electronic mail addresses in this example are
   reserved for documentation as described by [RFC2606] and do not
   identify operational refrigeration infrastructure.
7.  Relationship to Status Code 418
   Status code 418 was introduced by the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control
   Protocol [RFC2324] and is associated with an apparatus that is a
   teapot and therefore cannot brew coffee.  Status code 483 represents
   a distinct condition.
   A teapot might be neither a freezer nor a general-purpose server.
   Similarly, a freezer might contain an HTTP server without becoming a
   teapot.
   An implementation choosing between 418 and 483 SHOULD consider the
   immediate reason that the request cannot be satisfied:
   *  If the request cannot be satisfied because the responding
      apparatus is a teapot, 418 might be appropriate.
   *  If the request cannot be satisfied because the responding server
      is not a freezer, 483 might be appropriate.
   *  If the apparatus is both a teapot and not a freezer, the
      implementation SHOULD report the condition most directly relevant
      to the requested operation.
   This document does not define response prioritization for combination
   refrigerator-freezer-teapot appliances.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 6]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
8.  Distinguishing Refrigerators from Freezers
   A refrigerator is not necessarily a freezer.  An implementation MUST
   NOT advertise freezer capability merely because it can maintain a
   temperature lower than the surrounding environment.
   If a request specifies a target temperature, the server SHOULD
   evaluate its actual supported temperature range.  A server that can
   maintain 4 degrees Celsius but cannot maintain -18 degrees Celsius
   can return 483 when asked to preserve frozen food at -18 degrees
   Celsius.
   This document does not allocate a separate status code meaning "I'm
   Only a Refrigerator".  Such allocation is left for future work,
   preferably after an appropriate cooling-off period.
9.  Intermediaries and Cold-Chain Proxies
   An intermediary MUST NOT replace a 483 response with a success
   response unless it has arranged for the requested operation to be
   performed by a freezer-capable service.
   An intermediary that forwards a request to a freezer-capable service
   SHOULD preserve sufficient request information to maintain
   traceability through the cold chain.
   A proxy MUST NOT claim that a request has been frozen merely because
   it has been buffered, queued, archived, or stored on media described
   as cold storage.
   Intermediaries SHOULD NOT select a refrigeration service based only
   on the service name.  Capability claims ought to be authenticated
   before perishable or temperature-sensitive goods are redirected.
10.  Caching Considerations
   A 483 response is not heuristically cacheable.
   A 483 response can be cached when explicit freshness information
   permits caching, subject to [HTTP-CACHING].
   Implementations ought to use short freshness lifetimes when
   refrigeration capabilities can change.  A server might acquire
   freezer capability through appliance discovery, configuration,
   repair, attachment of suitable hardware, or relocation.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 7]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   A cache MUST include relevant request-selection information in its
   cache key when freezer capability depends on the requested product,
   target temperature, duration, physical location, or other request
   characteristics.
11.  Security Considerations
   A 483 response can disclose information about the physical
   capabilities of a server, appliance, building, warehouse, or
   logistics network.  Such information might assist an attacker in
   identifying facilities that lack refrigeration capability.
   Servers SHOULD avoid disclosing unnecessary details about appliance
   models, internal temperatures, stored contents, physical locations,
   maintenance schedules, or cold-chain topology.
   A malicious service might falsely claim freezer capability in order
   to receive physical goods, operational instructions, or sensitive
   inventory information.  Clients SHOULD authenticate services before
   relying on claims of refrigeration capability.
   Implementations MUST NOT treat the presence or absence of a 483
   response as proof that a physical item has been frozen, refrigerated,
   preserved, spoiled, thawed, or consumed.
   Request bodies associated with freezing operations might reveal
   dietary preferences, medical requirements, biological sample
   information, commercial inventory, or other sensitive data.
   Implementations SHOULD apply suitable confidentiality and access-
   control protections.
   Operators are advised not to troubleshoot servers by placing them
   inside domestic freezers.  Condensation, restricted airflow, thermal
   shock, and the objections of other freezer occupants can produce
   undesirable results.
12.  Privacy Considerations
   Requests involving refrigeration can expose information about food,
   medicine, scientific samples, commercial shipments, or household
   activity.  Servers SHOULD minimize the information returned in a 483
   response and SHOULD avoid echoing sensitive request content.
   Logs containing 483 responses SHOULD be protected according to the
   sensitivity of associated request metadata and content.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 8]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
13.  IANA Considerations
   This document requests that IANA register the following entry in the
   "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Status Code Registry":
               +=======+===================+===============+
               | Value | Description       | Reference     |
               +=======+===================+===============+
               | 483   | I'm Not a Freezer | This document |
               +-------+-------------------+---------------+
                    Table 1: Requested HTTP Status Code
                                Registration
   If the registration request is not approved, this section can itself
   be considered safely stored for future use, although not necessarily
   below freezing.
14.  Implementation Considerations
   Implementers are encouraged to use the exact reason phrase "I'm Not a
   Freezer" when a reason phrase is supported.  Clients MUST NOT depend
   on the reason phrase because HTTP semantics are identified by the
   numeric status code.
   Protocol versions that do not transmit a reason phrase can use status
   code 483 without modification.
   Implementations MAY include a machine-readable problem detail
   describing the unsupported refrigeration operation, subject to
   [RFC9457].
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: application/problem+json
   Cache-Control: no-store
   {
     "type": "https://example.com/problems/not-a-freezer",
     "title": "I'm Not a Freezer",
     "status": 483,
     "detail": "The requested temperature is outside supported capabilities."
   }
15.  Acknowledgments
   The author thanks the designers of HTTP, refrigeration equipment,
   electronic mail, and combination appliances for creating the
   conditions that made this clarification necessary.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 9]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   The peas used in the example were not harmed during preparation of
   this document, although their final temperature could not be
   independently verified.
16.  Normative References
   [RFC2119]  Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate
              Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119,
              DOI 10.17487/RFC2119, March 1997,
              <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2119>.
   [RFC8174]  Leiba, B., "Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC
              2119 Key Words", BCP 14, RFC 8174, DOI 10.17487/RFC8174,
              May 2017, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8174>.
   [HTTP]     Fielding, R., Nottingham, M., and J. Reschke, "HTTP
              Semantics", STD 97, RFC 9110, DOI 10.17487/RFC9110, June
              2022, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110>.
   [HTTP-CACHING]
              Fielding, R., Nottingham, M., and J. Reschke, "HTTP
              Caching", STD 98, RFC 9111, DOI 10.17487/RFC9111, June
              2022, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9111>.
   [RFC9457]  Nottingham, M., Wilde, E., and S. Dalal, "Problem Details
              for HTTP APIs", RFC 9457, DOI 10.17487/RFC9457, July 2023,
              <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9457>.
17.  Informative References
   [RFC2324]  Masinter, L., "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol
              (HTCPCP/1.0)", RFC 2324, DOI 10.17487/RFC2324, 1 April
              1998, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2324>.
   [RFC2606]  Eastlake, D. and A. Panitz, "Reserved Top Level DNS
              Names", BCP 32, RFC 2606, DOI 10.17487/RFC2606, June 1999,
              <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2606>.
Author's Address
   Ricardo Bánffy
   Email: rbanffy@gmail.com
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                 [Page 10]

      does not necessarily maintain them below the freezing point of
      water.
   Cold storage
      A term that might refer to refrigerated physical storage,
      infrequently accessed data storage, an offline cryptographic
      wallet, or other facilities that are insufficiently warm.  Use of
      the term does not establish freezer capability.
   Freezer-capable server
      An HTTP server associated with equipment that can perform the
      freezing operation requested by the client.  Merely operating
      inside a freezer does not necessarily make an HTTP server freezer-
      capable.
3.  The 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) Status Code
   This document extends the HTTP status-code semantics defined in
   [HTTP] with the 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) status code.  The status code
   indicates that the server understood the request but cannot satisfy
   it because the requested operation requires freezing or refrigeration
   capabilities that the server does not possess.
   A server MAY return 483 when all of the following conditions apply:
   *  The request can be parsed and understood.
   *  Satisfying the request would require the server to freeze,
      refrigerate, chill, or preserve a physical item by reducing its
      temperature.
   *  The server is not capable of performing the requested temperature-
      control operation.
   A server MUST NOT return 483 merely because:
   *  its operating temperature is below ambient temperature;
   *  it uses liquid, air, immersion, or phase-change cooling;
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 3]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   *  it provides a service described as "cold storage";
   *  one or more software processes have been frozen;
   *  its physical location is cold;
   *  its hostname contains words such as "freezer", "ice", "arctic",
      "frost", or "cold"; or
   *  it is unresponsive in a way informally described as "frozen".
   A 483 response SHOULD contain a representation explaining that the
   selected server lacks the required refrigeration capability.  Where
   appropriate, the representation MAY identify a freezer-capable
   alternative.
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: text/plain
   This server is not a freezer and cannot satisfy the requested operation.
4.  Client Behavior
   A client receiving a 483 response SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the
   same request to the same server unless it has reason to believe that
   the server has subsequently acquired suitable refrigeration
   capabilities.
   A client MAY attempt the request against another origin if that
   origin is known to be freezer-capable.
   A client MUST NOT interpret a 483 response as evidence that the
   server is a refrigerator.  The response communicates a lack of
   freezer capability and makes no claim concerning lesser, adjacent, or
   unrelated cooling capabilities.
   Clients SHOULD avoid automatically redirecting physical goods based
   solely on URI authority components, DNS names, electronic mail
   addresses, service banners, or unverified appliance metadata.
5.  Applicability
   Status code 483 is applicable when a request crosses a boundary
   between digital instructions and physical temperature-control
   operations.
   Examples include:
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 4]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   *  an HTTP-controlled kitchen appliance receiving a request to freeze
      food;
   *  an industrial control gateway receiving a request to preserve a
      sample below a specified temperature;
   *  a logistics service receiving an instruction that requires a cold-
      chain facility that it does not operate; and
   *  a general-purpose HTTP server receiving a request intended for a
      refrigeration appliance.
   Status code 483 is not intended to report CPU thermal throttling,
   data-center cooling failures, insufficient heat dissipation,
   unresponsive software, immutable data, object freezing in programming
   languages, or process suspension.
6.  Example: Electronic Mail Concerning Frozen Goods
   Consider an HTTP service that accepts electronic mail for delivery to
   suitable appliances.  A client might inadvertently attempt to deliver
   a message intended for a freezer:
   POST /mail HTTP/1.1
   Host: mail.example
   Content-Type: message/rfc822
   From: alice@example.com
   To: freezer@example.com
   Date: Tue, 3 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000
   Message-ID: <peas-483@example.com>
   Subject: Please freeze these peas
   Dear Freezer,
   Please maintain the attached peas at approximately -18 degrees
   Celsius until further notice.
   Regards,
   Alice
   If the selected service is not a freezer and cannot cause the
   requested freezing operation to occur, it MAY reject the request with
   status code 483:
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 5]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: text/plain
   This server is not a freezer and cannot satisfy the requested operation.
   An implementation MUST NOT infer refrigeration capability solely from
   an electronic mail address containing the strings "freezer",
   "refrigerator", "cold", "ice", or similar terminology.
   The recipient address identifies the intended appliance but does not
   prove that the HTTP service handling the message controls that
   appliance.
   The domain names and electronic mail addresses in this example are
   reserved for documentation as described by [RFC2606] and do not
   identify operational refrigeration infrastructure.
7.  Relationship to Status Code 418
   Status code 418 was introduced by the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control
   Protocol [RFC2324] and is associated with an apparatus that is a
   teapot and therefore cannot brew coffee.  Status code 483 represents
   a distinct condition.
   A teapot might be neither a freezer nor a general-purpose server.
   Similarly, a freezer might contain an HTTP server without becoming a
   teapot.
   An implementation choosing between 418 and 483 SHOULD consider the
   immediate reason that the request cannot be satisfied:
   *  If the request cannot be satisfied because the responding
      apparatus is a teapot, 418 might be appropriate.
   *  If the request cannot be satisfied because the responding server
      is not a freezer, 483 might be appropriate.
   *  If the apparatus is both a teapot and not a freezer, the
      implementation SHOULD report the condition most directly relevant
      to the requested operation.
   This document does not define response prioritization for combination
   refrigerator-freezer-teapot appliances.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 6]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
8.  Distinguishing Refrigerators from Freezers
   A refrigerator is not necessarily a freezer.  An implementation MUST
   NOT advertise freezer capability merely because it can maintain a
   temperature lower than the surrounding environment.
   If a request specifies a target temperature, the server SHOULD
   evaluate its actual supported temperature range.  A server that can
   maintain 4 degrees Celsius but cannot maintain -18 degrees Celsius
   can return 483 when asked to preserve frozen food at -18 degrees
   Celsius.
   This document does not allocate a separate status code meaning "I'm
   Only a Refrigerator".  Such allocation is left for future work,
   preferably after an appropriate cooling-off period.
9.  Intermediaries and Cold-Chain Proxies
   An intermediary MUST NOT replace a 483 response with a success
   response unless it has arranged for the requested operation to be
   performed by a freezer-capable service.
   An intermediary that forwards a request to a freezer-capable service
   SHOULD preserve sufficient request information to maintain
   traceability through the cold chain.
   A proxy MUST NOT claim that a request has been frozen merely because
   it has been buffered, queued, archived, or stored on media described
   as cold storage.
   Intermediaries SHOULD NOT select a refrigeration service based only
   on the service name.  Capability claims ought to be authenticated
   before perishable or temperature-sensitive goods are redirected.
10.  Caching Considerations
   A 483 response is not heuristically cacheable.
   A 483 response can be cached when explicit freshness information
   permits caching, subject to [HTTP-CACHING].
   Implementations ought to use short freshness lifetimes when
   refrigeration capabilities can change.  A server might acquire
   freezer capability through appliance discovery, configuration,
   repair, attachment of suitable hardware, or relocation.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 7]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   A cache MUST include relevant request-selection information in its
   cache key when freezer capability depends on the requested product,
   target temperature, duration, physical location, or other request
   characteristics.
11.  Security Considerations
   A 483 response can disclose information about the physical
   capabilities of a server, appliance, building, warehouse, or
   logistics network.  Such information might assist an attacker in
   identifying facilities that lack refrigeration capability.
   Servers SHOULD avoid disclosing unnecessary details about appliance
   models, internal temperatures, stored contents, physical locations,
   maintenance schedules, or cold-chain topology.
   A malicious service might falsely claim freezer capability in order
   to receive physical goods, operational instructions, or sensitive
   inventory information.  Clients SHOULD authenticate services before
   relying on claims of refrigeration capability.
   Implementations MUST NOT treat the presence or absence of a 483
   response as proof that a physical item has been frozen, refrigerated,
   preserved, spoiled, thawed, or consumed.
   Request bodies associated with freezing operations might reveal
   dietary preferences, medical requirements, biological sample
   information, commercial inventory, or other sensitive data.
   Implementations SHOULD apply suitable confidentiality and access-
   control protections.
   Operators are advised not to troubleshoot servers by placing them
   inside domestic freezers.  Condensation, restricted airflow, thermal
   shock, and the objections of other freezer occupants can produce
   undesirable results.
12.  Privacy Considerations
   Requests involving refrigeration can expose information about food,
   medicine, scientific samples, commercial shipments, or household
   activity.  Servers SHOULD minimize the information returned in a 483
   response and SHOULD avoid echoing sensitive request content.
   Logs containing 483 responses SHOULD be protected according to the
   sensitivity of associated request metadata and content.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 8]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
13.  IANA Considerations
   This document requests that IANA register the following entry in the
   "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Status Code Registry":
               +=======+===================+===============+
               | Value | Description       | Reference     |
               +=======+===================+===============+
               | 483   | I'm Not a Freezer | This document |
               +-------+-------------------+---------------+
                    Table 1: Requested HTTP Status Code
                                Registration
   If the registration request is not approved, this section can itself
   be considered safely stored for future use, although not necessarily
   below freezing.
14.  Implementation Considerations
   Implementers are encouraged to use the exact reason phrase "I'm Not a
   Freezer" when a reason phrase is supported.  Clients MUST NOT depend
   on the reason phrase because HTTP semantics are identified by the
   numeric status code.
   Protocol versions that do not transmit a reason phrase can use status
   code 483 without modification.
   Implementations MAY include a machine-readable problem detail
   describing the unsupported refrigeration operation, subject to
   [RFC9457].
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: application/problem+json
   Cache-Control: no-store
   {
     "type": "https://example.com/problems/not-a-freezer",
     "title": "I'm Not a Freezer",
     "status": 483,
     "detail": "The requested temperature is outside supported capabilities."
   }
15.  Acknowledgments
   The author thanks the designers of HTTP, refrigeration equipment,
   electronic mail, and combination appliances for creating the
   conditions that made this clarification necessary.

Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   The peas used in the example were not harmed during preparation of
   this document, although their final temperature could not be
   independently verified.

articles.title: How Will AI Affect Open Source Development?
articles.body:
How Will AI Affect Open Source Development? (linuxfoundation.org) 32
			
		 	
				This week the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) announced it would broaden its AI security resources, including a new guide to finding and fixing vulnerabilities using AI, "from preparing and sandboxing AI to validating, fixing, and preventing issues."  The guide "stresses that AI-generated patches should never be trusted without automated tests and human review. An online course (LFD126) is planned for the coming months."
OpenSSF also released the State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026 report (supported by OpenSSF, ActiveState and the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation). And it turns out the 2026 report "found a growing gap between the pace of AI-driven software development and organizations' ability to secure the code being produced."
 58% of surveyed teams ship code faster than security reviews can keep up, while 60% say AI coding assistants have increased the number of external packages in their codebases. This data underscores the importance of trusted, reliable guidance as AI deployment continues to grow. 
Meanwhile the Linux Foundation announced at this week's Web Summit that it was releasing a new study on "how commercial open source companies generate revenue, convert users into customers and build their businesses," emphasizing the question's new relevance in the age of AI.  "AI now writes code almost for free, and that raises a hard question for the whole software industry: if code costs next to nothing, where does the value of software lie?"
Commercial open source [COSS] companies have been answering that question for more than 30 years. They have built large businesses on code they give away, which makes them a good guide to how software will make money in the age of AI...  Seventy-two percent of respondents report a net positive impact from AI, against 8% negative. So far, the gains show up mostly inside companies. Internal productivity is the most cited benefit (73%), ahead of market expansion (46%) and new monetization opportunities (39%). AI roles are the only hiring category growing on net.
COSS strategy is mostly unchanged by AI. But when companies do adapt, they are nearly twice as likely to open more of their core product rather than become more closed.  When asked what sets them apart, 57% of companies name brand recognition and trust, well ahead of enterprise features, integrations and community size. They turn that trust into revenue through support and services (63%), managed cloud (49%) and open core (43%). Most combine these: 65% run two or more revenue models. 
Companies stack models as they grow, rather than switching between them: managed cloud rises from 35% of companies below $5 million ARR to 66% above $20 million. Venture-backed companies lean toward open core (53% vs. 38% for others). 
The report draws on a survey of 225 commercial open source founders and enterprise leaders (published by Linux Foundation Research in partnership with Serena,  and with sponsorship from AWS, Red Hat, Futurewei and the  Cloud Native Computing Foundation.  And when it comes to open source, "over half of founders point to brand recognition and community trust as their greatest asset," said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.  So
"The findings from this year's report prove that AI isn't a threat to commercial open source software — it's an accelerating tailwind.  With 72% of companies viewing AI as a net positive primarily driving internal productivity, the ecosystem is leaning further into collaboration." 
The Linux Foundation's announcement includes an interesting perspective from Matthieu Lavergne, partner at the venture capital company Serena.  "Open source won the developer. Next, it will win the agent. The 225 founders we surveyed mostly see AI as a productivity gain today, but that's only the start: agents are set to become open source's largest users, and they choose what is open, proven and trusted. The founders who build and price for these new users will define the infrastructure of the AI era."

articles.title: Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China?
articles.body:
Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China? (cnn.com) 42
			
		 	
				In three years "Megaspeed International" went from from inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary "to one of Asia's biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US," reports CNN.
"It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks," trade data investigator William George told CNN. 
As Nvidia's Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, "Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia," CNN writes, noting scrutiny of the company from the Singapore government and US officials "concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers..."
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia's most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China's tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.  US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those...   [T]rade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia... Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year... 
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company's server purchases and their final destinations.   In a statement, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence that Huang had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information "to downplay her role" at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws. A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.  
CNN reminds readers that Jensen Huang accompanied US President Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, and also lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports.  "The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue."
"However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well," they add.  And the Taiwanese government is even seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, "as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong."

articles.title: Pranksters Redirect Bitly's Links in X Posts for Trump, McDonald's and Burger King
articles.body:
Pranksters Redirect Bitly's Links in X Posts for Trump, McDonald's and Burger King (kwwl.com) 15
			
		 	
				"A massive link-hijacking scheme has turned corporate social media archives into bizarre and offensive redirects," reports the New York Post:
Posts from high-profile accounts — including fast-food giants McDonald's and Burger King, as well as President Donald Trump — are getting hacked, with over decades-old links suddenly redirecting users to unrelated website links including links about 9/11 and the Holocaust.
An unknown party appears to be taking control of expired Bitly link shorteners — a widely used URL-shortening and link-management service — and altering their destinations....
Another Burger King tweet from July 13, 2011 — reading, "Now it's even easier to eat right at BURGER KING® restaurants with @WeRRestaurants. All you need is a zip code!" — was warped to link straight to Adolf Hitler's Wikipedia page... Two posts on Donald Trump's X account were also altered: a 2013 post redirected to a "Baby Fortnite" page, while a 2012 post linked to a video of Mario and Luigi from Super Mario Bros.
 
The article notes that about 20 of Trump's old X posts had "switched" links, including some now pointing to videos of the Transformers.  And it adds that "outraged web users are also slamming Bitly over its flaw that allows links to 'die' and be recycled by pranksters and bad actors."
"Links dating as far back as 2009 from URL-shortening service Bitly were affected," reports CNN, "and only corporate and political X accounts appear to have been targeted, with President Donald Trump's personal account seemingly hit the hardest."  "Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and former Vice President Mike Pence... were also hit to varying degrees."
Bitly said Sunday afternoon in a post on X that it had "identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts." The company said it suspended the accounts that altered links and were working to disable the affected URLs...   It's unclear whether hackers made custom Bitly links, which effectively allow them to copy the original URL and redirect to any website. That may have been possible if the original Bitly link to the website no longer exists or has expired.... Another 2013 post from Trump tagged former Republican nominee for president Mitt Romney, and links to the popular game "Geometry Dash"....
A post in 2011 by Trudeau contains a Bitly link that redirects to a vulgar YouTube audio clip...   Government accounts have also been ironically affected. A 2012 post from the FBI about computers infected by "Ghost Clicks" now directs to a page with a photo of a seal, while the Department of Defense account had a separately redirected post.

articles.title: Old Bitly Links Are Being Hijacked
articles.body:
Update, 15 November, 23:40 UTC: CNN reports redirected Bitly links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense as well. Our third check of the Trump links, at 23:35 UTC, found nothing new: 49 links re-created years after their tweets still work.
Update, 15 November, 22:30 UTC: Bitly has confirmed the problem. In a post on X at 19:13 UTC it said it had identified an issue that “allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links” and send people to unrelated content. Bitly said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links. It added that its Trust and Safety team is working on protections against similar misuse.
Update, 15 November, 19:30 UTC: The Burger King and McDonald’s links no longer redirect. Both were still working at 15:05 UTC and returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page by 19:22 UTC. The same has happened to the two extra Trump links we verified and to six of the seven links in our sample that pointed somewhere new. The seventh now shows a Bitly warning that the account that created it has been suspended. The 49 re-created links that look like the originals still work.
Burger King’s X account was not hacked. A Bitly short link in a tweet the chain posted on 24 July 2011 was registered again by someone else on 15 November 2026 and pointed at Wikipedia’s list of Nazi concentration camps. The tweet was advertising a restaurant locator. A post quoting it passed 2 million views within hours, and Burger King’s original has since become unavailable.
It was not the only one. Eighteen minutes earlier a Bitly link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was registered the same way and pointed at Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Ransomnews also checked 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, taken from a public archive. Bitly’s own link pages show that 56 were created after the tweets they sit in, and a 57th is blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam. Four were registered on 15 November. Two more, created in January 2024 and January 2025, point at domains that copy the names of crypto services.
In brief
- Burger King posted the tweet on 24 July 2011 with the short link bit[.]ly/19BFiM. Bitly’s information page for that link gives a creation time of 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 and a destination on Wikipedia.
- A link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011, bit[.]ly/mLWJO0, was created again at 05:14 UTC the same morning, 18 minutes before Burger King’s. It opens Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Both tweets have since become unavailable.
- Nobody posted from either company’s account. The links changed hands on Bitly’s side, so the old tweets send readers wherever the new owners choose.
- Of 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, 40 are still the original. Another 49 were created again later but lead where the tweets suggest, 48 of them in a 17-minute run on 26 May 2023. Seven lead somewhere else and one is blocked by Bitly.
- Four of those seven were registered on 15 November 2026 between 07:49 and 09:57 UTC. They open a Roblox profile, a YouTube video (twice) and a Wikipedia article about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein.
- One Trump tweet from April 2011 carries three links to videos of his children. All three have been replaced.
- Bitly’s help pages say the ending of a bit.ly link cannot be reused, even after the account behind it is deleted. In February 2025 it was reported to have fixed a bug that allowed this.
- We found no public statement from Bitly, Burger King or McDonald’s by 14:30 UTC on 15 November.
- By 19:22 UTC both links returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. None of the seven Trump links that pointed somewhere new redirects any more.
- Bitly confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC. It said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links.
- CNN reported the same evening that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense were affected too. We have not checked those links ourselves.
Was Burger King hacked?
No. Nothing was posted from Burger King’s account and nothing suggests anyone got into it. The tweet is 15 years old and reads as it always did, pointing followers to “our handy restaurant locator” through a Bitly link. What changed is where that link goes. As with the Microsoft 365 outage three days earlier, the first question people asked was whether it was an attack on the company, and the answer is the same.
Bitly keeps a public information page for every short link. Add a plus sign to the end of the address and it shows where the link points and when it was created. For bit[.]ly/19BFiM that page gives the destination as Wikipedia’s “List of Nazi concentration camps” and the creation time as 15 November 2026, 05:32 UTC. A link printed in a tweet from 2011 can only carry a 2026 creation date if the same ending was issued a second time.
We tested the method on links nobody disputes. A link whose creator says he made it in 2009 shows a 2009 creation date. A custom link tweeted by a YouTube channel on 21 June 2017 shows 20 June 2017. Among the Trump links that are still original, 32 of 40 were created on the day of the tweet or the day before.
The post that spread it came from an X user at 06:51 UTC, 79 minutes after the link was created, and had 2.2 million views by early afternoon.
By 13:45 UTC the Burger King post inside it was showing as unavailable. We do not know whether Burger King removed it or X did. The short link was still redirecting to Wikipedia at 13:47 UTC.
Was McDonald’s hacked?
No. Its link was changed 18 minutes before Burger King’s. On 7 June 2011 McDonald’s tweeted a Bitly link to something its team in Sweden had done. Bitly’s information page for bit[.]ly/mLWJO0 shows the link was created at 05:14 UTC on 15 November 2026, and it redirects to Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. The tweet was returning a not-found error when we checked at 14:20 UTC.
The two changes are close in time and alike in style. The X user Alex Greenland, who spotted both timestamps, thinks one person or group is probably behind them. Nothing we have seen proves that.
How does an old Bitly link get hijacked?
Someone registers its ending again. The part of a Bitly link after the slash is called the back-half. Bitly generates one at random, or the user types a custom one. If an old link stops existing and its back-half can be claimed, whoever claims it decides where every tweet, email, PDF and printed QR code carrying that link now leads. No password is stolen and no account is touched, so the brand that posted the link sees nothing wrong.
Bitly says this cannot happen. Its help page on deleted accounts states that bit.ly links keep working and that their back-halves “cannot be re-used”, whether they were generated or custom. A separate page says Bitly deletes accounts that have been inactive for three years. The creation dates we collected do not fit the first statement. Back-halves that appear in tweets from 2009 to 2012 belong to links created between 2023 and today.
It has happened before. In February 2025 Disruptionist reported that memecoin promoters had taken over Bitly links in 2013 posts by Donald Trump and Melania Trump and pointed them at token listings. According to that report, a bug let people claim a back-half once the original link or its account had been deleted or deactivated, and Bitly fixed it and switched off the hijacked links. Links created on 15 November 2026 show the same thing is possible now.
The X user Damin Toell identified it as link hijacking at 07:25 UTC and noted that old Trump posts were affected too.
At 09:18 UTC another user described the method in a post that has been viewed more than 46,000 times. Three more Trump links were registered in the 40 minutes that followed.
Free tool
How does your own site score?
Run the same forty passive checks against your own domain: TLS and certificates, security headers, SPF and DMARC, cookies before consent, and what your stack quietly reveals. A grade out of 100 in about fifteen seconds.
No signup. Nothing installed. We only request what your site already serves publicly.
How many old links have been replaced?
More than half of the ones we tested. We took every tweet Donald Trump’s account posted from 2009 to 2016 from the Trump Twitter Archive data set on GitHub, left out retweets and extracted the bit.ly links.
