- Lack of experience scheduling and managing complex software. Even with so much work on the table, several early contributors were already interested in the project and willing to put real time into helping write code. Unfortunately, I had very little teamwork experience back then (being completely self-taught and only three years into programming altogether), so I failed to turn that interest into effective contributions. That sank in much deeper once I started working in industry: 3 or 4 of my coworkers can split up responsibilities, stand up a project from scratch in 2 to 3 months, and ship it to production, whereas I had poor instincts for project planning and mostly just wrote whatever was on my mind at the moment. Open-source volunteer bandwidth can’t be compared to a full-time job, of course, yet the truth is I didn’t do a great job of building a community or pushing the project forward.
Early 2026 to July 2026: The turning point came when coding agents led by Claude Opus 4.6 started catching on. I began using agents to help with the mountain of tedious detail work and painful cross-platform debugging, and found they were remarkably good at it. During this stretch I did a sweeping cleanup of the existing codebase and established the prototype of clice as it stands today. As agents grew stronger, I handed them increasingly complex tasks and kept moving the project forward rapidly. It was an exciting period: I could finally stop burning hours on tedious details and focus on architecture and feature work. At the same time, it hit me that coding agents were only going to keep getting stronger. If humans stop writing code altogether in the future, what point does a language server even have? That pushed me to start designing and building clice’s CLI features.
July 2026 to present: By July I felt the timing was right to put out early test builds and iterate based on real user feedback. Core language server features were already in place and fully usable day to day, though still short of everything I had originally envisioned, so I threw myself into building out the rest of that vision, tuning performance, and fixing bugs. In October, I started planning clice’s modular self-hosting. That was a remarkably complicated undertaking, because C++ module support today is a long, painful story:
- CMake supports modules, yet if implementation units importing a module use different compile flags, CMake forks a separate compilation of the module even when those flags don’t affect PCM compatibility. CMake also has no built-in compilation cache, which matters a lot for CI; normally we reach for ccache to solve that, except ccache doesn’t support modules.
- clice has a demanding platform matrix: six combinations across Windows/Linux/macOS × ARM64/x64, plus ASan builds, prebuilt LLVM/Clang binaries to speed up CI, C++23 import std, and build artifacts that depend only on system libraries rather than extra shared libraries so everything works out of the box for users.
I surveyed the options extensively, and the answer was that an out-of-the-box setup for this simply did not exist in open source, and most open-source C++ module projects don’t have build requirements nearly this involved. After thinking it through carefully, I built xclang, inspired by zigcc, to give every target platform a unified cross-compilation experience, and paired it with Bazel (which includes built-in build caching) to solve the build problem for good. Going one step further, I wrote clice modularize to automatically generate module wrappers for every third-party library we depend on, completing clice’s self-hosted modularization! That probably makes clice one of the most complex open-source C++ projects using modules today.
Alongside all of this, I ran extensive fuzz testing across many open-source projects and fixed a huge number of bugs, bringing clice to genuine production readiness!
What about agents?
As I mentioned earlier, I designed a CLI interface for clice so that it would still hold some value in the agent era. An obvious idea is replacing grep with clice query: it is more accurate and uses fewer tokens. That is true, except exact symbol lookup requires indexing the whole project first, which takes a very long time. grep is imprecise, sure, yet 2 or 3 grep calls are usually enough to find the target, and the extra text grep pulls back isn’t necessarily a bad thing for helping an agent understand the codebase. Put plainly, most of this CLI isn’t actually all that useful. The part that really earns its keep is probably clice modularize: if you ask an agent to modularize a project on its own, it spins up a swarm of subagents and writes custom scripts to pull off the migration, which is both slow and expensive. Giving the agent clice modularize to assist the migration works much better. LLMs are trained first and foremost for generality, and what they do best is writing and combining scripts to generalize across problems. As things stand, only highly specialized tools still carry real value; otherwise you are usually better off letting the LLM compose its own scripts.
As agents keep getting stronger, especially with models led by Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, the cost of building complex software keeps falling, and 10x or even 100x the productivity of the past is well within reach. Over on X, you can see plenty of people asking Claude in a single sentence to rewrite the TypeScript compiler in another programming language and getting better performance out of it. Surprising at first glance, yet completely reasonable when you think about it. Software written in the past was bounded by human time, cost, and skill, so codebases inevitably accumulated lots of suboptimal code paths. When humans optimize performance, we go after the main bottlenecks, whereas an agent can tirelessly optimize every path until the small wins add up. Refactoring also often produces a better architecture than existing code; rewriting or refactoring software was just too expensive to justify before. In the foreseeable future, then, most code may be written entirely by agents, humans may stop writing code and even reading it (which is already happening now), and language servers may have no reason to exist at all. Agents might even invent programming languages better suited to themselves: compilation and interpretation themselves have often become the bottleneck in the agent loop, and agents already have the ability to optimize that underlying infrastructure; they just haven’t started yet. Ideally, every stage of the agent loop should be something the agent itself can improve and speed up, compilers and toolchains included.
To be continued
That is a sad reality, and in an era like this it means the effort I poured into clice over the past two and a half years is unlikely to have the lasting meaning I first imagined. Every time I dwell on it, I slip into a dark mood, bordering on nihilism. I can’t help asking myself: thousands of hours and a lot of money, and what was it all for?
Because I taught myself programming off the beaten path without a CS degree, I got used early on to the cycle of finding my own goals, defining problems, solving them, and then looking for the next goal. Interest alone only sustains me for a little while; sticking with something for the long haul takes some deeper “meaning” or “vision” behind it, ideally one I defined for myself. And now that meaning is fading away. So over the past few months, I started pushing myself relentlessly. The more those thoughts crept in, the harder I used agents to drive the project forward, trying to finish it before it lost its meaning altogether.
Imagine an alternate timeline where coding agents never took off. clice wouldn’t be nearly as complete as it is today, of course, yet I would have slowly gained experience, learned how to collaborate and plan work, built a community around it, and watched clice move forward slowly and steadily. Except the SOTA models have already been trained. Models like Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are real, and whether AI is a bubble or not, they aren’t going away. Software becoming cheap is already an undeniable fact.
We have to face reality, so what mindset should we bring to all of this? My thinking has shifted again recently, though honestly neither my mental state nor my daily life is in a great place right now. Pouring yourself too deeply into one thing naturally takes a heavy toll when it doesn’t turn out the way you hoped. Still, if you zoom out over a longer stretch of time, what does it really amount to? Even if I had done nothing at all for these two and a half years, so what? There is plenty of life ahead. I know that in principle, yet letting go is hard, especially when this project has been part of my life for over two years. As I mentioned in an earlier post, graduating from college never really felt real to me, because the rhythm of my life barely changed afterward: apart from my job, it was just this project. Something has to change eventually, though. I can treat clice as my graduation project: my real graduation project, not one from the chemistry major I never really liked. And that’s enough. I don’t need to force a grander meaning onto it. This graduation project has met every single goal I set two years ago, and exceeded them by a wide margin. It stands on its own as the best illustration of modern C++, neatly bringing together everything I studied about C++ in college. If on top of that it can be helpful to people just learning to program or curious about modern C++, that is plenty.
So this post is a kind of ritual for me. I need to step out of my old life and look for other things worth doing, maybe things outside code. I will keep maintaining clice, just not at the intensity I used to; practically everything worth building is already built anyway, so from here on it will mostly be incremental optimizations and bug fixes based on user feedback. In times like these, it is hard to say what the right path is, or what you ought to be doing. Nobody knows what will happen next week, let alone next year, or how far AI will actually go. I think it is time to rest for a while so I don’t burn out, and have the energy to face whatever problems come next. I still have a strong drive to keep creating good work. It just might not be about programming anymore, and figuring that out is what I need to learn and think through in this next stage.
That’s all for this post. Thanks for reading. I hope you’ll give clice a try, and feel free to report any problems!

articles.title: What Picasso taught me about building AI Agents
articles.body:
The great master Pablo Picasso is famously attributed with saying:
"It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child."
His work, Le Taureau (The Bull), captures this beautifully. Across 11 iterations, Picasso progressively stripped away the details of a bull until only a few lines remained. Yet the bull was unmistakable.
In my journey of learning to build AI agents, I can relate. It has come full circle.
Like many engineers, I started with abstractions and sophisticated software systems. Frameworks, orchestration engines, multi-agent architectures, state machines, vector databases, memory systems, and elaborate planning mechanisms.
The more I experimented, the more I found myself stripping things away.
The models were getting better. More things worked with a single prompt. But that wasn't the whole story. I had been overcomplicating things.
This is now my workflow.
I open my terminal.
mkdir my_awesome_agent
cd my_awesome_agent
claude
and start a conversation.
"Claude, I want to build an agent that does XYZ. Help me initialize it. Create an AGENTS.md and let's figure out what else it needs."
I work through a few questions with Claude.
What is this agent supposed to accomplish?
What is the actual job? Not what framework to use, unless you're creating a framework. What does success look like? What decisions can the agent make independently? What should it never do without permission?
What skills does it need?
Skills are specialized instructions that can be reused and remixed. There are plenty of excellent examples on the internet. Borrow them, adapt them, combine them, or ask Claude to create new ones.
Often, a skill is simply a Markdown file with instructions and perhaps a few supporting resources.
What context does it need?
The agent will need context: what your business does, who your customers are, how your codebase works, or some domain-specific knowledge. These can all live as Markdown files inside the folder. Some context can be retrieved when needed. Some comes from the conversation itself. You don't automatically need a vector database or a sophisticated memory architecture.
What tools does it need?
To perform a job, an agent needs tools. Maybe it needs to search the web, read a database, call an API, execute a script, or interact with a browser.
Introducing a tool is as simple as enabling a plugin or adding an MCP connector.
I ask Claude to help identify the smallest set of tools required to accomplish the task. A tool could even be created dynamically, with the agent writing and invoking code. The agent could also find tools on the internet and install them.
How does the agent get invoked?
For an agent to be useful, it needs to be invoked as part of a workflow, whether by a cron job, a webhook event, or another program.
The simplicity is in the packaging. A folder with instructions is a clean deployable unit. It can be versioned, copied around, and embedded in other processes.
With Claude and the required tools and credentials available, it can be invoked headless using the -p flag:
cd my_awesome_agent
claude -p "Do awesome stuff"
Headless means there is no interactive chat. Claude receives the task, works in the agent's folder, prints the result, and exits. A script can pass in the task and collect the output. For unattended work, I configure the tool permissions in advance. Claude can also return structured JSON for another program to use.
Anthropic's documentation on headless execution covers the commands and configuration.
When the agent starts, it needs to know where to find its instructions, what input it has received, and whether it should resume previous work. The invocation mechanism can change without changing the fundamental purpose of the agent.
This setup can be deployed on a remote VM, with hooks triggering the agent and a tunnel providing access to a service that invokes it.
How does it know whether it has done a good job?
This is where things have drastically improved. I can now get things done with a single prompt, without elaborate instructions. Nowadays, I often just trust it to get on with the job. And I expect it to keep getting better.
When it gets something wrong, I go through it with Claude. What happened? What was missing? What should we change?
Claude saves local session transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl. Each transcript records the conversation, tool calls, and tool results. It provides a trace of how the task unfolded: what Claude was asked to do, what it tried, what came back from the tools, and where errors appeared.
Claude can then be pointed at the transcript and asked to analyze the run. Where did it go off track? Did it miss an instruction, lack context, or misinterpret a tool result? What evidence in the trace supports that explanation? That gives us something concrete to examine before deciding what to change.
If the lesson is reusable, we save it in the instructions, context, examples, or tests.
Over time, the agent improves. Not necessarily because its underlying model has changed, but because its working context and operating instructions have become better.
How do we know it is improving?
To be rigorous about the implementation, you need benchmarks: representative tasks with clear criteria for success. Running the same tasks lets you compare your agent across harnesses such as Gemini CLI, Codex, or pi, or across models such as Opus, Astra, Sol, and DeepSeek. It also tells you whether changes to your own setup are helping.
These tests are called evals. This is probably the hardest part of all of this. I will share my experiences with evals in a later post. In the meantime, these writeups explain them in much more depth:
- Hugo Bowne-Anderson: Does Your AI Agent Actually Work? A Guide to Evals
- Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar: AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know
Orchestration
A task can be broken into smaller tasks and delegated to specialized subagents. In this setup, each subagent has its own folder under the main agent, containing its instructions, context, and tools.
The root agent acts as an orchestrator, or chief of staff. It decides which subagent to invoke, gives it a task, and brings the results together. For example, a chief-of-staff agent could coordinate all kinds of activity across a company, delegating work to specialist agents.
Making this concrete
I am using this setup to publish this website, including the article you are reading. For this project, I am using Codex.
The agent works in the website's project folder. AGENTS.md points it to my editorial guidance and publishing instructions. Those files capture my preferences and the steps for updating the site. Here is a shortened view of the actual folder:
claramap/
├── AGENTS.md
├── docs/
│   ├── editorial-memory.md
│   └── publishing.md
├── content/posts/
│   └── what-picasso-taught-me-about-building-ai-agents.md
├── public/assets/blog/
└── scripts/
    ├── build.mjs
    └── check-live.mjs
The agent is connected to Cloudflare through MCP, so it can deploy the site as part of the workflow.
For this article, I asked it to add the orchestration section and create the chief-of-staff diagram. It edited the Markdown, generated the illustration, built the site, deployed to Cloudflare, and checked the live page.
The publishing instructions also cover Google Analytics and discovery files. The build automatically updates the site's analytics tracking code for its current pages, regenerates llms.txt and llms-full.txt, and updates the RSS feed.
I review the result and correct it in the same conversation. Change the wording. Move a diagram. Make an image bigger. Reusable feedback goes back into the editorial memory, so future runs have better instructions to work with.
The Essence
This is the foundation. Everything else builds on this.
No need for OpenClaw, Hermes, Muse, LangChain, Pydantic, or any other agent framework. Solve the basic case first, then add machinery later. You can find leads, create content, publish, send emails, answer questions, fill out forms, or write code. Pick a job. Give it what it needs. Let it work.
Like Picasso's bull, my approach became simpler as I learned what to leave out. The progression looks something like this.

Thus, it aims to be a comprehensive handbook that atheists can use to support, enrich, and scrutinize their perspective.

articles.title: Jensen Huang allegedly manufactured the GPU shortage
articles.body:
- 0-20%: Unlikely - Lacks credible sources
- 21-40%: Questionable - Some concerns remain
- 41-60%: Plausible - Reasonable evidence
- 61-80%: Probable - Strong evidence
- 81-100%: Highly Likely - Multiple reliable sources
75%
Probable
Now that NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang is no longer the company CEO, we have some truth behind the exponential rise of semiconductor and memory prices. According to the latest findings, it appears that we were led to believe that there was an organic supply shortage, but in reality, we learn that Jensen was actually leveraging NVIDIA’s own balance sheet to finance AI startups and datacenter buildouts so they could absorb the company’s over-ordered semiconductor shipments from TSMC.
NVIDIA faced an “avalanche” of excess TSMC silicon and memory, and the only way to curb the oversupply was to fund AI startups
The fresh revelations stem from a tense August 2026 confrontation between Huang and NVIDIA’s longtime Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, now the interim CEO. Seeing as how the former head honcho was escalating the GPU maker’s financial exposure, Kress pushed to rein in the company’s “circular financing” commitments to smaller cloud providers and major AI firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Initial discussions had floated underwriting roughly 8 gigawatts of OpenAI compute valued at up to $250 billion, and Kress successfully scaled NVIDIA’s signed guarantee cap down to roughly 4.25 gigawatts, or up to $125 billion. As a result, Jensen reportedly belittled Kress for questioning the deals, referring to her as “a deer in the headlights.”
To justify NVIDIA's need to financially underwrite OpenAI and smaller cloud operators to keep them purchasing its GPUs, Huang privately admitted that major cloud giants were pivoting away from NVIDIA in favor of in-house custom chips. With hyperscalers actively reducing their reliance on “off-the-shelf parts,” Huang acknowledged that the massive volume of prepaid TSMC wafers and memory NVIDIA had committed to buying was “coming at him like an avalanche.”
By funding datacenter expansion for AI startups, NVIDIA effectively created artificial demand to clear out its own surplus silicon instead of letting the supply flood the market and force GPU prices down. Those internal pressures align with earlier assessments from industry analyst Ed Zitron, who estimated that at least $200 billion worth of NVIDIA AI GPUs are sitting idle in warehouses after being purchased by cloud giants that lacked either the electrical grid capacity or immediate end-user demand to power them on. Amazon faced a similar dilemma.
Knowing that the imminent avalanche would be upon NVIDIA sooner rather than later, the company reportedly contacted TSMC to wind down its upcoming chip orders. For PC builders and hardware enthusiasts who have endured years of steep GPU and RAM pricing under the impression of severe component scarcity, the disclosures shatter the shortage narrative and expose the aggressive financial maneuvering used to keep hardware prices elevated.
While Jensen can’t be faulted for making these moves because he was keeping the best interests of the company in mind, it’s a stab in the back for gamers and hardware owners who are unable to locate any mouth-watering deals for GPUs or memory because of the perceived shortage.
News Source: The Wall Street Journal
Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

articles.title: Disk encryption on NetBSD – achieving secrecy
articles.body:
Threat models
These are two threat models for which disk encryption is the answer:
- The device is stolen or lost and its contents must remain secret.
- The device is tampered with, and all attempts at tampering must render it unusable.
Right now, we will focus on the first threat model. It is very difficult to build a tamper-proof system, and you need to worry about tamper-proofing your hardware, depending on what kind of actor is a realistic threat.
If we want to keep data on the system secret, we must first consider which data is worth protecting. On a NetBSD system, our data can be grouped into two broad categories:
- System files (open source software)
- User-modified files
Does the /bin/sh executable downloaded from the NetBSD FTP server contain any sensitive information?
On a BSD system, due to the separation of the base system and packages, many root file system directories are mostly unmodified outside of upgrades. In a properly configured system, nearly all system daemons and user applications are not going to be running as root, so won’t have permission to modify or create files in /bin.
We can reasonably assume that /bin/sh is the same binary that every other NetBSD user is running. A user may even opt to make directories containing such system files read-only.
Problems with disk encryption
The operating system needs to be able to load files to boot.[citation needed] This makes "true" full disk encryption difficult to achieve without specialized hardware, since the user needs some way to enter a password or an encryption key, and can’t do so without some form of software running on their computer. NetBSD also needs to store some amount of metadata about the encrypted partition on the disk, such as information on how to generate a secure 256-bit key from a 24 character password.
It is common for Unix systems to use shared libraries, which are loaded by programs to access system functionality. If these become unavailable, for example, by /usr/lib going missing, it becomes much harder to use the system. Familiarize yourself with the standard utilities in /rescue which don’t need working shared libraries to be useful.
The cryptographic algorithms that get standardized by the US government tend to be slow when implemented in software. This carries a performance penalty. As a result, many modern CPUs include implementations of ciphers like AES in hardware. For those that don’t, there’s alternative ciphers like Adiantum.
Which directories are sensitive?
And which are necessary for the OS to load?
On a normal NetBSD system, several directories have a high chance of being modified during system operation:
- 
/home - user-specific files
- 
/var - log files, system-wide databases (e.g. mail notifications), crash dumps…
- 
/root - configuration files relevant to the root user account
- 
/usr/pkg and /usr/local - where third-party software is installed
- 
/etc - init scripts, system-wide configuration for the base system
A simple approach might be to encrypt /home. However, this might not be enough for some users. Although the crash directory can be easily changed with
sysctl,
a crash dump contains a snapshot of system memory which might be sensitive. If any servers have been run on the system, the log files might be sensitive. Mail sent to users (e.g. about their interrupted vi sessions and associated backups) might reveal sensitive file names.
Some users opt for the
cgdroot
approach, which uses only a small unencrypted ramdisk to pivot to an encrypted file system. However, this modifies the system startup routines significantly and may make certain rescue options harder. So, it’s worth asking whether there’s an approach that is somewhere in the middle, and still uses the standard NetBSD installation and boot process. Many BSD systems use separate file system partitions for /usr and /var, and this is a standard configuration supported by the NetBSD installer.
/etc is a harder problem to solve, since it contains files necessary to boot the system. However, on a typical desktop system, many files in /etc remain untouched. Passwords in /etc are generally stored only in hash form, except for Wi-Fi access points and certain VPN configurations (although it’s easy to reconfigure wpa_supplicant_flags to use a different configuration file from the default one in /etc). Many configuration files are only loaded much later in the boot process, after /usr is already mounted, and can easily be replaced with symbolic links to files on another file system.
The installation process
The NetBSD installer has basic functionality, but gets the job done quickly. In this configuration, we’re going to install NetBSD to a small unencrypted root file system. When you start to ignore the growth that can occur in /usr and /var and /home, even a complete NetBSD installation with development tools included is tiny. 4 GB should be more than enough.
For example purposes, I am going to use a sparc64 virtual machine, but the process is basically the same for more mainstream CPU architectures like amd64.
The installer detects that we already have a partitioned disk. We’re going to pick the "e: Delete everything" option so we have a fresh disk to start with:
Next, we’re going to choose "Set sizes of NetBSD partitions". This will allow us to have a small root, and reserve a large encrypted partition:
Here, I’ve decided I want a 4096 MB (4 GB) root file system, and a 11263 MB (11 GB) partition allocated for /var. Later, we’ll make /usr and /var share a disk partition, so don’t worry about this too much. Select "Go on".
On the next screen, I’ve changed the type of the secondary partition to "cgd" (listed under "Other type"), NetBSD’s encrypted device driver. I’ve also set its mount point to "-" so we can reconfigure it later:
I tell the installer I want to do a Full Installation and it completes as normal, installing everything into the small root partition.
When we reboot and log in as root, we enter a new world… our 4 GB unencrypted root partition.
Post-installation setup (disklabel)
Since I’m on sparc64, the disk is partitioned into disklabels. wd0 is the primary drive, and the disklabel command shows that /dev/wd0d is the partition reserved for our encrypted file system:
# disklabel wd0
#        size    offset     fstype [fsize bsize cpg/sgs]
 a:   8389584         0     4.2BSD      0     0     0  # (Cyl.      0 -   8322)
 b:   2097152   8389584       swap                     # (Cyl.   8323 -  10403*)
 c:  33554432         0     unused      0     0        # (Cyl.      0 -  33288*)
 d:  23067072  10487232        cgd                     # (Cyl.  10404 -  33287)
We can go directly ahead with creating a parameters file for the cgd:
# cgdconfig -g -k argon2id -o /etc/cgd/wd0d adiantum 256
And then load the configuration and set our password:
# cgdconfig -V re-enter cgd0 /dev/wd0d

The next time we enter our password, we want to be able to verify that the password was correct, to avoid reading or writing invalid data.
This is done by choosing a verification method based on the contents of the encrypted partition. For flexibility’s sake, we’re going to put another disklabel inside the encrypted partition. This will allow the system to easily verify the password is correct by looking for a valid disklabel, but also gives us flexibility in our choice of file system.
# disklabel -i cgd0

First, it asks for a file system type. Enter ? to display a list of types:
partition>a
Filesystem type [unused]: ?
Supported file system types:
Since I’m running -current and want to test the Log File System, I’m going to enter "4.4LFS". A more common and well-tested configuration would be "4.2BSD".
Next is the start offset and partition size:
Start offset ('x' to start after partition 'x') [0c, 0s, 0M]: 0
Partition size ('$' for all remaining) [0c, 0s, 0M]: $
Since "a" is the only sub-partition at the moment, the default start of 0 is fine. "$" will use all available space on the cgd.
Finally, we’ll save our new label and quit the disklabel editor:
partition>W
Label disk [n]?y
Label written
partition>Q

and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:
cgd0 /dev/wd0d /etc/cgd/wd0d

# newfs -O2ea /dev/rcgd0a

# mkdir -p /encfs
# mount /dev/cgd0a /encfs
Add a new line in /etc/fstab for our encrypted mount point:
/dev/cgd0a      /encfs  lfs     rw,noatime      1 2
Use "ffs" instead of "lfs" if you aren’t using the Log File System. If using FFS, you may want to use the options rw,log,noatime to enable journaling.
Post-installation setup (disk wedges)
On a recent amd64 machine, your system probably uses GPT and disk wedges instead of disklabels. Assuming our primary disk is ld0, we can see a list of wedges with dkctl:
# dkctl ld0 listwedges
/dev/rld0: 3 wedges:
dk0: 20e57277-ad70-408e-9c68-225270ed1500, 9267072 blocks at 64, type: ffs
dk1: abad5a2d-8411-4d36-980e-a5f2b03a1047, 4194304 blocks at 9267136, type: swap
dk2: 2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661, 53647360 blocks at 13461440, type: cgd

# cgdconfig -g -k argon2id -o /etc/cgd/maincgd aes-cbc 256
And then load the configuration and set our password:

Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.

Now change the verify_method in /etc/cgd/maincgd to gpt,
and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:
cgd0 NAME=2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661 /etc/cgd/maincgd
For now, we’ll only create one partition inside the new sub-table. I’m running -current and want to test the Log File System, so I’ll use the "lfs" partition type. A more common and well-tested configuration would be "ffs".
# gpt add -l encfs -t lfs cgd0
You should receive a kernel message, readable with the dmesg command, which notes that a new wedge is available, including its number. In this case, it’s dk3.
For it to be useful, we’ll need to create a file system on it. Once again, here I’m using the Log File System:
# newfs_lfs /dev/rdk3
A more normal and well-tested configuration would use FFSv2ea:
# newfs -O2ea NAME=encfs
We can now mount and access the encrypted file system:
# mkdir -p /encfs
# mount NAME=encfs /encfs
Add a new line in /etc/fstab for our encrypted mount point:
NAME=encfs /encfs       lfs     rw,noatime      1 2
Use "ffs" instead of "lfs" if you aren’t using the Log File System. If using FFS, you may want to use the options rw,log,noatime to enable journaling.
Final steps (moving over the data)
These are required regardless of whether using disklabel or wedges.
We’re going to copy our important directories to the new encrypted file system:
# umount /var/shm
# cp -a /home /var /usr /encfs/
We need to create a symbolic link with ln because the /usr/lib directory contains some relative links to ../../, and it expects the lib directory to be there at the root. This is a hack:
# ln -s /lib /encfs/lib
Then, we move our important directories out of the way and replace them with links to the encrypted ones:
# /rescue/mv /home /home2
# /rescue/ln -s /encfs/home /home
# /rescue/mv /var /var2
# /rescue/ln -s /encfs/var /var
# /rescue/mv /usr /usr2
# /rescue/ln -s /encfs/usr /usr
Finally, we need to add a line to /etc/rc.conf to tell it to mount the encrypted partition early, so that /usr and /var are available during the init process:
# echo 'critical_filesystems_local="/encfs"' >> /etc/rc.conf
Disclaimer
After this process, the NetBSD installer is not aware of the encrypted partition existing during upgrades. Online upgrades must be used, rather than offline upgrades where the installer is booted from removable media. This may be done with a tool like sysupgrade.
This guide was 100% written by one human and might contain human errors.

articles.title: Disk encryption on NetBSD – achieving secrecy
articles.body:
Threat models
These are two threat models for which disk encryption is the answer:
- The device is stolen or lost and its contents must remain secret.
- The device is tampered with, and all attempts at tampering must render it unusable.
Right now, we will focus on the first threat model. It is very difficult to build a tamper-proof system, and you need to worry about tamper-proofing your hardware, depending on what kind of actor is a realistic threat.
If we want to keep data on the system secret, we must first consider which data is worth protecting. On a NetBSD system, our data can be grouped into two broad categories:
- System files (open source software)
- User-modified files
Does the /bin/sh executable downloaded from the NetBSD FTP server contain any sensitive information?
On a BSD system, due to the separation of the base system and packages, many root file system directories are mostly unmodified outside of upgrades. In a properly configured system, nearly all system daemons and user applications are not going to be running as root, so won’t have permission to modify or create files in /bin.
We can reasonably assume that /bin/sh is the same binary that every other NetBSD user is running. A user may even opt to make directories containing such system files read-only.
Problems with disk encryption
The operating system needs to be able to load files to boot.[citation needed] This makes "true" full disk encryption difficult to achieve without specialized hardware, since the user needs some way to enter a password or an encryption key, and can’t do so without some form of software running on their computer. NetBSD also needs to store some amount of metadata about the encrypted partition on the disk, such as information on how to generate a secure 256-bit key from a 24 character password.
It is common for Unix systems to use shared libraries, which are loaded by programs to access system functionality. If these become unavailable, for example, by /usr/lib going missing, it becomes much harder to use the system. Familiarize yourself with the standard utilities in /rescue which don’t need working shared libraries to be useful.
The cryptographic algorithms that get standardized by the US government tend to be slow when implemented in software. This carries a performance penalty. As a result, many modern CPUs include implementations of ciphers like AES in hardware. For those that don’t, there’s alternative ciphers like Adiantum.
Which directories are sensitive?
And which are necessary for the OS to load?
On a normal NetBSD system, several directories have a high chance of being modified during system operation:
- 
/home - user-specific files
- 
/var - log files, system-wide databases (e.g. mail notifications), crash dumps…
- 
/root - configuration files relevant to the root user account
- 
/usr/pkg and /usr/local - where third-party software is installed
- 
/etc - init scripts, system-wide configuration for the base system

Some users opt for the

approach, which uses only a small unencrypted ramdisk to pivot to an encrypted file system. Many BSD systems use separate file system partitions for /usr and /var, and this is a standard configuration supported by the NetBSD installer.
/etc is a harder problem to solve, since it contains files necessary to boot the system. However, on a typical desktop system, many files in /etc remain untouched. Passwords in /etc are generally stored only in hash form, except for Wi-Fi access points and certain VPN configurations (although it’s easy to reconfigure wpa_supplicant_flags to use a different configuration file from the default one in /etc). Many configuration files are only loaded much later in the boot process, after /usr is already mounted, and can easily be replaced with symbolic links to files on another file system.

articles.title: 50th Anniversary of 'Star Wars' Celebrated with iMax 70mm Re-Release, Special Events, New Movie
articles.body:
50th Anniversary of 'Star Wars' Celebrated with iMax 70mm Re-Release, Special Events, New Movie (deadline.com) 46
			
		 	
				"Lucasfilm and Disney have restored the original Star Wars (1977) and will release the film in multiple formats, including Imax 70mm [starting February 19], as part of the franchise's 50th anniversary celebrations," reports Deadline.
The original film will also be displayed in its original 16:9 format on the center of Cosm's 12K+ LED Dome, in a special presentation developed with Disney, Lucasfilm, ILM, and MakeMake.  They're calling it a "Shared Reality production" where "the surrounding visual environments dynamically evolve to immerse the audience in iconic Star Wars locations and moments."
Deadline reports more 50th anniversary celebrations
In addition to the Imax 70mm screenings, the film will also be presented in Digital Imax, Digital Cinema, 70mm, 35mm, and 4DX.    On May 4th, 2027, Lucasfilm will release a new behind-the-scenes documentary, The Hero Awakens, from filmmaker R.J. Cutler on Disney+.   Star Wars events already on the calendar for 2027 include Shawn Levy's [movie]  Star Wars: Starfighter, which will be released May 28. 
There's also a new poster paying homage to the original 1977 film, reports the Disney news site Mickey Visit, plus a newly orchestrated score by John Williams that they assume "will be used on all the projects that debut this year."
On April 2-3, [Disney] will debut the new "Star Wars in Concert: The Skywalker Saga" at the Hollywood Bowl. The show will be hosted by Anthony Daniels, known for his role as C-3PO.  Special performances of John Williams' iconic film scores will feature scenes and music from all nine Skywalker Saga films. The concert is a sweeping celebration of the stories, themes, and music that have inspired audiences around the world for five decades...
They also teased that new and legacy licensees — including Hasbro, the LEGO Group, adidas, Mars, Aston Martin, Steinway, Hajime Sorayama presented by Complex, and more — will introduce 50th-anniversary collections... In the opening of the press release, Disney mentioned that as part of the announcements there will be "reimagined Disney Parks and Cruise Line offerings."
  
The article adds that the April's Star Wars Celebration at the Los Angeles Convention Center has already sold out.
There's more Star Wars news, writes long-time Slashdot reader schwit1
A light saber used by Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" movies The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold Thursday for nearly $5 million in an auction.   The light saber, which was used in the climactic duel in Cloud City in which Vader tells Luke Skywalker "I am your father" sold for $4.875 million at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by Heritage Auctions. The sale marks a world auction record for any "Star Wars" collectible, according to the auction house. 
The previous record was Heritage's $3,750,000 sale of Luke Skywalker's lightsaber and severed hand effects rig on July 15, 2026.  And they're still auctioning more Star Wars memorabilia...

articles.title: A Human Reads the Anthropic IPO Filing
articles.body:
Supported by
A Human Reads the Anthropic I.P.O. Filing
The prospectus is unparalleled in its willingness to discuss existential risk. But does honesty bring comfort?
My breath taken, I looked up from my desk to gaze at the red-orange blanket of fallen leaves just outside my window. I needed the pause, or maybe the distraction, from what I was reading.
The thick document before me looked like any other standard business proposal: a prospectus for an initial public offering with boilerplate language about dividends, compensation and Class A stock. But the more I read, the more it morphed into experimental literature, equal parts business plan, philosophical treatise and sci-fi thriller.
This will be an I.P.O. unlike any other, its language both matter-of-fact and unnerving, its ultimate subject our future. Not futures, as in the stock market, but the future, as in what it might look like and whether we have one.
The prospectus comes from Anthropic, the artificial intelligence concern immersed in the technologies rapidly transforming the human experience. It is poised to offer shares to the public for the first time, and this document, recently filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, lays out its blueprint for potential investors to decide whether to bet on the future of civilization.
I cannot give you odds on this existential gamble. My prior awareness of Anthropic extended little beyond clicking on a button with hundreds of thousands of other writers to join a massive class-action copyright lawsuit. As someone who knows next to nothing about investments, I read the Anthropic prospectus solely out of my vested interest as a human being.
In seeking the considerable capital needed for chips, data centers and electricity, the company — with an estimated valuation well north of $1 trillion — begins its pitch by dangling the possibility that artificial intelligence could “solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.”

articles.title: The MacBook Pro's OLED PWM Problem: When a 'Better' Display Becomes Worse to Use
articles.body:
The MacBook Pro’s OLED PWM Problem: When a ‘Better’ Display Becomes Worse to Use
Apple has made a spectacular display. But spectacular isn’t the same as comfortable, and the people discovering that distinction deserve to be heard.
Apple has brought tandem OLED technology to the MacBook Pro, joining the Mini-LED display that has served the range since 2021 (and which Apple continues to sell). Apple calls this a “PROLED XDR Display”. It features individually illuminated pixels, effectively infinite contrast, wonderfully deep blacks and the sort of image quality that Mini-LED, for all its considerable strengths, can’t fully equal. Peak HDR brightness has increased, and Apple has introduced a new display engine designed to manage colour, luminance and pixel usage with extraordinary precision. And of course, in a first for any Apple notebook display, it has touch-input capability.
When Apple unveiled the new MacBook Pro, the initial reaction to the screen was overwhelmingly positive.
But there’s a burgeoning discussion taking place within the Mac community that deserves attention. On MacRumors forums, a thread titled RIP MacBook Pro PROLED for PWM Sensitive Eyes - apple cmon! has attracted people describing remarkably similar experiences. Discussions are also appearing across Reddit, with owners describing discomfort shortly after using their new machines. Some report headaches; others describe a strange sensation of eye fatigue, dizziness, nausea, or an inability to concentrate on the screen for extended periods. Some have already returned the device.
Mike Wuerthele, of AppleInsider, published an article on 10 November titled If you’re getting dizzy using PROLED MacBook Pro, you are not alone, examining these reports.
The following caveat probably doesn't need to be made, but I will make it anyway: these are individual experiences, not evidence that the new MacBook Pro is causing problems for everyone. Plenty of owners are likely perfectly content with (and dazzled by) their new displays. But that isn’t really the point. For the people experiencing these symptoms, the fact that somebody else can happily spend several hours staring at the same screen isn’t particularly reassuring, especially given Apple's long-standing commitment to accessibility. A display can be technically spectacular and still be a spectacularly poor display for a subset of people.
PWM
Much of the discussion centres on Pulse Width Modulation, or PWM. It’s a technique used to control screen brightness by rapidly switching or modulating the light output. On an OLED display, the pixels themselves produce the light, rather than relying on a separate backlight. By varying the way that light output is modulated, the display can control its apparent brightness.
At sufficiently high frequencies, this flickering isn’t something most people can consciously detect. But some people are particularly sensitive to this kind of modulation and can experience eye strain, headaches and other forms of discomfort when looking at displays that use it.
This is a pretty good demonstration of PWM on an M4 iPad Pro, which also has a tandem OLED display:
Neither PWM nor the discussion surrounding it is new. It’s been a talking point for years, particularly around OLED displays, and something manufacturers have increasingly had to consider as display technology has evolved (including Apple — more on this later).
Notebookcheck, which conducted laboratory testing of the 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, measured PWM at 240Hz. This is its worst-case reading, with flickering detected at brightness settings of 99% and below.
To put that into perspective, the M4 Pro MacBook Pro with Mini-LED display measured 14,880Hz in Notebookcheck’s testing. At 240Hz, the brightness fluctuation repeats 240 times per second; at 14,880Hz, it repeats almost 15,000 times per second. That’s one hell of a difference. The reported modulation frequency of the new MacBook Pro’s OLED panel is roughly 62 times lower than that measured on the Mini-LED model.[1]
Frequency isn’t the only consideration, though. The extent to which brightness fluctuates during each cycle also matters, as do the characteristics of the display’s dimming system. We shouldn’t assume that these figures translate directly into how comfortable somebody will find a particular display. There’s no simple, one-size-fits-all formula for predicting who will experience problems.
It’s also worth avoiding the temptation to treat PWM as a universal explanation for every headache or instance of eye strain. Screen discomfort can have numerous causes. Some users’ discomfort may have nothing to do with PWM.[2]
Wait, isn’t OLED supposed to be better?
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is emphatically not an inexpensive laptop with a budget screen. This is Apple’s flagship professional notebook. The PROLED XDR configuration represents a substantial investment, and the display is arguably its most important selling point. Apple has spent years refining its displays, and there’s a reasonable expectation that moving to OLED should represent some sort of improvement in almost every meaningful respect, especially given the savagely high price tag of these new machines.
PWM isn’t exclusive to OLED. LCD displays can use it, too, including Mini-LED displays. The difference is that OLED panels often use PWM as part of their brightness-control behaviour, and manufacturers have considerable flexibility in how they implement it. Some OLED displays use relatively high-frequency modulation; others use a combination of PWM and DC (Direct Current) dimming to manage brightness.
DC dimming generally involves reducing the current supplied to the display rather than relying entirely on rapidly switching the light output on and off. It’s often considered preferable for people who are sensitive to PWM. But the presence of DC dimming doesn’t necessarily mean PWM has been eliminated. The new MacBook Pro appears to use a combination of PWM and DC dimming. Notebookcheck notes that DC dimming is present across brightness levels, but that the panel still exhibits 240Hz flickering.
The people who didn’t have a problem before
One of the problems with PWM discussions is that they tend to quickly become highly polarised. Someone says they experience headaches, and someone else responds that they’ve been using OLED displays for years without any issues. Two things can be true at once.
The most important aspect of this discussion, to me, is the number of people insisting they had no difficulty using OLED devices prior to using this new MacBook. This matters because PWM sensitivity is often discussed as though it’s a straightforward, binary distinction between people who can tolerate OLED and people who can’t. That binary distinction doesn’t exist. Sensitivity exists along a spectrum.

Someone who has been happily using an OLED iPhone Pro for several years might find a different OLED screen uncomfortable; someone who has experienced headaches with one OLED laptop might have absolutely no problem with another. And there is a distinction between OLED technology itself and the particular implementation of OLED in this particular MacBook.
To give an example, someone on the PWM_Sensitive subreddit posted this about their experience with the new MacBook Pro (shared with their permission):
I was really surprised I was affected by this. Have been looking at various OLED screens for years and did not expect to have issues.
Then I got my PROLED 16 inch last week and during the first few hours I thought I just had a bad day. Now it’s so obvious. As soon as I look at the screen I get lightheaded, I feel like I am floating away … and when I then get up and start walking, I feel dizzy for like an hour or two, then it gets better again. But as soon as I look at the screen for more than a minute, the dizziness comes back.
This is first machine in 20 years as an Apple customer that I return literally anything. Too bad, because the laptop is amazing in all aspects otherwise, I was in love with it the moment I took it out of the box (coming from an M1 Pro 16 inch). It would have been my daily driver for the next 5 years. So, now I am waiting for the M7 variant and hope they will find a way to mitigate this issue. I am returning the MacBook tomorrow morning after less than a week of using it.
Apple has built up a loyal audience of professional Mac users who spend enormous amounts of money on the machines, and enormous amounts of time in front of their displays. Photographers, designers, developers, writers and video editors can spend entire working days looking at a MacBook screen (I do). So imagine upgrading from an M4 or M5 Pro MacBook Pro with Mini-LED, expecting a more beautiful version of something you already love, only to discover that you can’t comfortably use the new machine for more than a short period. Good customer experience is usually Apple's guiding North Star. Bad customer experience is usually Apple’s Kryptonite.
Has Apple compromised on the wrong thing?
There are plenty of engineering considerations involved in developing a tandem OLED panel for a laptop — brightness, power consumption, thermal management, longevity, colour accuracy and uniformity all have to be balanced.
Apple's displays have always involved trade-offs to one degree or another. Take the Mini-LED display — while it's truly excellent in many respects, it notoriously suffers from blooming (an inherent limitation of Mini-LED local dimming) and has also typically had poor pixel response times. These are compromises Apple has had to accept in order to deliver the particular combination of brightness, contrast and HDR performance that makes the Mini-LED display so impressive.
Apple has made some ambitious claims about the new PROLED XDR display, particularly around its brightness and the intelligence of its display engine. We don’t know why Apple has ended up with this particular dimming behaviour, or what trade-offs were involved in achieving it. But I think it’s reasonable to ask whether display comfort received enough consideration in the process. The new MacBook Pro produces extraordinary blacks, stunning HDR highlights and exceptionally accurate colours, and so on. But none of that matters particularly much if the person sitting in front of it develops a headache, or feels like they want to throw up when they're using it.
When the majority experience isn’t everyone’s experience
People experiencing unusual, poorly understood or relatively uncommon health problems have often found themselves struggling to be heard — they have to explain their symptoms repeatedly, defend their experiences and convince others that their difficulties are genuine. I don't personally know anybody who suffers from PWM sensitivity, and I appreciate that it can be difficult for someone without these experiences to understand how something so ordinary could become a source of physical discomfort for another person. But personal experience shouldn't be a prerequisite for compassion. We don’t need to experience somebody else’s symptoms to acknowledge that they are struggling.
Stories like this tend to surface only once an ill-defined and arbitrary threshold of people complaining is crossed. But even if something only affects a small minority, doesn’t that minority matter? Apple certainly appears to care about the minority — they put an extraordinary amount of work into accessibility features, many of which are incredibly important to relatively small groups of users. It’s one of the things which sets Apple apart. Features such as VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch and other accessibility technologies exist because Apple recognises that different people interact with technology in different ways. Why shouldn’t display comfort receive similar consideration? It doesn’t mean Apple must abandon OLED, or compromise the experience for everyone. It means offering alternatives where technically feasible.
Apple previously introduced a ‘Display Pulse Smoothing option’ on supported iPhone models. It’s an accessibility setting which can be toggled in the Settings app. Apple describes Display Pulse Smoothing as a way to create a smoother dimming experience at low brightness on supported iPhones. Its support documentation cautions that disabling PWM may affect low-brightness display performance under certain conditions. It took Apple a long time to include this feature by the way (it arrived nearly 8 years after the iPhone X was released). Incidentally, Apple has also included Display Pulse Smoothing on the new iPad mini with OLED display.
Could something similar be offered on the Mac? We shouldn’t assume that a software feature would completely resolve the issue. Changing the way the display is driven could introduce other compromises, and Apple would need to implement it carefully. But even a degree of user control would be gratefully received.
For now, anyone concerned about PWM sensitivity should be cautious about buying the new machine without trying it first. A quick demo in an Apple Store isn’t necessarily representative of spending an entire working day in front of the display. Don’t assume that being comfortable with an OLED iPhone means you’ll be comfortable with this MacBook. If you experience discomfort, don’t assume that increasing brightness or changing colour settings will necessarily resolve it.
The existing Mini-LED MacBook Pro thankfully remains a viable alternative for people who have found that display comfortable. But the Mini-LED MacBook Pro might not stay around for much longer. Apple looks to be transitioning to OLED across their devices — this may have consequences unless Apple changes the way they're implementing this particular technology.
The best MacBook display isn’t necessarily the best display for everyone
We sometimes get so caught up in the pursuit of better specifications that we forget what these devices are actually for. The most important part of a display is that it's something you sit in front of for hours at a time.
Displays to my mind are like mattresses — they're not something you should compromise on, unless financial constraints demand it. I've often been puzzled why people baulk at paying a lot for a display when they’re likely going to be using it for several hours a day. Similarly, I’ve often wondered why people baulk at paying a lot of money for a mattress, when they’re going to be spending roughly a third of their lives lying on one. A decent mattress is probably something you should invest in. The specs of the mattress matter, of course, and individual comfort matters enormously. The same thing is true with a display, which is why I have no issue having spent the money I did on a Studio Display XDR.
And this is what's so problematic with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display. According to many reviewers this is one of the best displays they've ever seen, and it has a price to match. Starting at £2899 for the 14-inch version (£3399 for the 16-inch), boy is it expensive. If the technology responsible for making the PROLED XDR Display look spectacular also makes it uncomfortable for some people to use, then we need to ask if that trade-off is worth it.
I suspect most people buying the new MacBook Pro will never think about PWM. They’ll open the lid, admire the display and get on with their lives. But for the people who have discovered that they can no longer comfortably use the latest MacBook Pro, this is a really big deal.
I’d like to see Apple explain why the new display behaves so differently from the Mini-LED panel used in other MacBook Pro models, and whether there’s any possibility of improving its dimming characteristics through software. Perhaps there’s a perfectly reasonable engineering explanation. Perhaps there are limitations inherent in this particular panel.
I’d be interested to hear from anyone who has experienced this first-hand, particularly those who have previously used Apple’s OLED iPhones or iPads without difficulty, but are now struggling with the new MacBook Pro.
Get in touch at hello@macanorak.com
You can also submit feedback to Apple here: https://www.apple.com/feedback/macbook-pro/
- A 62-fold difference in frequency doesn’t translate into a 62-fold difference in comfort. It doesn’t work that way. Frequency, modulation depth and individual sensitivity all matter. ↩︎
- It may have to do with what type of screen they’ve opted for — glossy, or nano-texture. A personal example here: I have the nano-texture screen on the MacBook Pro, my iPad Pro and my iPhone Duo, and I get along with those just fine. But I could not get along with nano-texture on Apple's range of Studio Displays — it caused me a lot of visual discomfort / headaches — moving to glossy screens with those monitors has treated me much better in that regard. ↩︎
