articles.title: Things That Turbo Pascal Is Smaller Than (2011)
articles.body:
It's not about technology for its own sake. It's about being able to implement your ideas.
Turbo Pascal 3 for MS-DOS was released in September 1986. Being version 3, there were lesser releases prior to it and flashier ones after, but 3 was a solid representation of the Turbo Pascal experience: a full Pascal compiler, including extensions that it made it practical for commercial use, tightly integrated with an editor. And the whole thing was lightning fast, orders of magnitude faster at building projects than Microsoft's compilers.
The entire Turbo Pascal 3.02 executable--the compiler and IDE--was 39,731 bytes. How does that stack up in 2011 terms? Here are some things that Turbo Pascal is smaller than, as of October 30, 2011:
The minified version of jquery 1.6 (90,518 bytes).
The yahoo.com home page (219,583 bytes).
The image of the white iPhone 4S at apple.com (190,157 bytes).
zlib.h in the Mac OS X Lion SDK (80,504 bytes).
The touch command under OS X Lion (44,016 bytes).
Various vim quick reference cards as PDFs. (This one is 47,508 bytes.)
The compiled code for the Erlang R14B02 parser (erl_parse.beam, 286,324 bytes).
The Wikipedia page for C++ (214,251 bytes).
(If you liked this, you might like A Personal History of Compilation Speed.)
permalink October 30, 2011
I'm James Hague, a recovering programmer who has been designing video games since the 1980s. Programming Without Being Obsessed With Programming and Organizational Skills Beat Algorithmic Wizardry are good starting points. For the older stuff, try the 2012 Retrospective.

articles.title: Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
articles.body:
Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.
Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
Following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy Congress wants to crack down.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.
Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

articles.title: Parents pay $75k for Alpha's AI school. Half of its students missed math target
articles.body:
Alpha School, the network of AI-driven private schools charging parents up to $75,000 a year, has won backers from Silicon Valley to the Trump administration. Its own data show most of its students aren’t reaching the model’s central promise.
Only 42% of Alpha students met the network’s goal of learning twice as fast in both math and reading, according to internal data first reported by The New York Times. The findings land as Alpha pushes into public schools, where districts are adopting its software in hopes of fitting more learning into less time.
What Alpha promises parents
Alpha has no traditional teachers. It employs what it calls “guides,” whose job, according to the company’s marketing materials, is to “make every student feel valued and motivated.” Guides don’t plan lessons or grade homework, Fortune reported in September.
The core of the pitch is that students will “learn twice as much as their peers in two hours of academics a day” using TimeBack, an app Alpha markets as an AI tutor. Cofounder MacKenzie Price says the app personalizes and accelerates learning for each student, freeing the rest of the school day for workshops on skills such as public speaking and relationship building.
The network has grown fast. A spokesperson told Fortune in September that Alpha had more than 1,200 students. The Times put the figure at about 1,500 across roughly 50 campuses, in line with the expansion plans Alpha announced in August.
That pitch has drawn AI optimists. “I definitely think using AI well is a skill in the future, if not the skill, so it’s kind of a disservice not to have that in school,” Sarah Cone, a venture capitalist whose 8-year-old daughter attends Alpha’s New York campus, told Fortune in September.
In September 2025, U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon toured Alpha’s Austin campus and called its model “the most exciting thing I’ve seen in education in a long time.” LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and hedge fund manager Bill Ackman have both publicly backed Price and Alpha on X. Even the X account of Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder serving more than 11 years in prison for fraud, praised Price.
Where students are falling short
Math is the bigger gap. About half of K-8 students at Alpha’s private campuses missed the goal of learning math twice as fast, and roughly one in five missed their reading targets, according to the Times‘ review of the network’s data.
Students who started behind fared worse. About a fifth of Alpha’s private school students scored at or below the 50th percentile nationally in math last fall, and only 37% of that group met the network’s 2x growth goal by winter, the Times found.
The two-hour premise is also in question. Guides and parents told Wired that students worked late into the night to meet the school’s goals. One parent of a 13-year-old reading at an 11th-grade level said reaching those goals came with “stress and anxiety.”
Former employees told 404 Media that Alpha’s AI generated faulty lesson plans, which internal documents said sometimes did “more harm than good,” and that the company scraped other online courses without permission.
Alpha’s model is reaching public schools
More than 2,600 public school students in Texas and South Carolina now use Alpha’s platform, according to company documents reviewed by the Times. That is a tougher test: public schools can’t remove struggling students, the Times noted, and they lack the prize incentives Alpha uses at its private campuses.
The Houston Independent School District, the largest in Texas, is piloting the software at two schools. Superintendent Mike Miles told the Times that students spent more time on Alpha’s apps than planned, cutting into other activities. He still wants AI in the district’s toolkit, calling it an important tool for students to be “successful in a different world and workplace.”
Research points to a learning penalty
Alpha’s expansion comes as schools grapple with falling math and reading scores and growing evidence that how students use AI matters as much as whether they use it.
A study of 26,811 secondary students in central China found that homework scores rose 18% after students adopted generative AI tools, while closed-book exam scores fell 20%. The OECD’s latest PISA results found that daily AI users scored lower in science than nonusers, while moderate users performed about the same.
Professors have told Fortune that students who lean on AI summaries struggle with sustained reading. “Today, if you assign that amount of reading, they often don’t know what to do,” Timothy O’Malley, a theology professor at the University of Notre Dame, told Fortune‘s Preston Fore in June.
“It’s not even an inability to critically think,” Jessica Hooten Wilson, a professor of great books and humanities at Pepperdine University, told Fortune. “It’s an inability to read sentences.”

articles.title: 'Birdbrain' Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can
articles.body:
Supported by
‘Birdbrain’ Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can
In a recent experiment, crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys.
Lemmy and Iggy, two carrion crows, are no strangers to a psychology lab. As study participants, they have helped scientists prove that birds can use tools to forage, learn numbers and count objects, and provided other insights into the ways birds think.
Now, they’ve also revealed that birds can make staggeringly quick decisions, besting their human and nonhuman primate counterparts with ease. In new findings published in Science, the crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys, quantifying the neural speed of avian decision-making for the first time.
The discovery might be the final blow for the use of “birdbrains” as a pejorative.
“We wouldn’t think of birds making these decisions faster than monkeys, or faster than us ‘awesome’ human beings,” said Mike Colombo, a neuroscientist and comparative psychologist at the University of Otago in New Zealand who was not involved in the research. “But they do. They’re just incredibly fast.”
Questions of bird intelligence have long been debated by researchers. Their small and superficially simple brains led scholars in the 19th and much of the 20th century to conclude they were not cognitively competent creatures. Even early research into birdsong, which demonstrated that some birds are capable of complex speech-like patterns and impressive vocal mimicry, was not enough to turn the tide. Their elaborate melodies were considered specialized adaptations that didn’t reflect their cognitive abilities.
Although passionate birders may find those conclusions obviously mistaken, the scientific community has been slower to catch on. “It’s taken the last 20 years to realize that actually their brain architecture is quite fascinating,” said Dr. Colombo.
Recent research, for example, has found that pigeons are capable of distinguishing between cancerous and noncancerous cells, numerical values, and words and non-words. Corvids (the group that includes crows, ravens, rooks and scrub jays) can even recognize themselves, solve abstract problems, plan for the future and show theory of mind — an ability to understand what other birds might be thinking and act accordingly.

articles.title: Show HN: A tiny macOS app that turns off the MacBook display [free license]
articles.body:
Blackout turns off your MacBook’s built-in display when you are working on an external monitor. System settings will not show the internal display as a desktop anymore. Unplugging monitors or closing the app will return to normal state again.
Use the switches above to see how your displays appear in macOS.
This works perfectly on Apple Silicon Macs (M-series), but on Intel Macs you'll still see the internal display listed on this system preferences page (macOS limitation).
Individual display switches
Switch individual displays on or off from one window.
Keep the lid open
Use your MacBook’s keyboard and trackpad with its screen dark.
Automatic reset to default
If something goes wrong, the app will automatically reset the screens to default (all screens are on)
Minimal footprint
Reduce the app to a tiny top menu bar icon, without an icon in the dock
Detects monitor disconnects
If monitor cable is unplugged, the app will detect this and act accordingly
TouchID keeps working
Unlike other tools, login or authentication via TouchID will work even with the display turned off.
No, as Apple doesn't allow software that uses the Apple hardware API in the App Store, probably to protect normies from breaking their systems. This app is officially signed by Apple with my valid Apple Developer account, so it's safe to use.
What happens when I close the app, restart the Mac, the app crashes, or I unplug the monitor cable?
In all these cases the internal display will be turned on with 80% brightness instantly. Also when macOS updates or other such events happen.
Is this a permanent change?
No, everything is just software-based, so whatever happens, your display will be back online after a macOS restart anyways.
Compatibility
The community is testing many devices, and this table will get updates.
All devices should work. Intel machines and base M3 MacBook / M3 MacBook Air have a hardware bug that MIGHT prevent turning off the internal display.

articles.title: FAA Router In Middle-of-nowhere Arkansas Identified as Cause of Nationwide Flight Chaos
articles.body:
FAA Router In Middle-of-nowhere Arkansas Identified as Cause of Nationwide Flight Chaos (nypost.com) 18
			
		 	
				Though the nationwide flight-grounding ended Friday, "Nearly 2,300 flights in the U.S. have been cancelled Sunday in the aftermath..." reports ABC News.    "Additionally, some 18,689 flights were delayed, per FlightAware."
But "a single malfunctioning FAA router in rural Arkansas appears to have caused the air travel chaos,"
reports the New York Post:
The problem originated at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a newly installed router flooded the network with excessive data traffic, disrupting communications between pilots and air traffic controllers, the Wall Street Journal reported. "We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds," Rebecca Guy, the FAA's technology chief, said on Saturday. ..   [U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean] Duffy said the failure occurred during routine maintenance to replace aging copper telecommunications with fiber-optic cables — part of a broader effort to modernize the FAA's outdated infrastructure.  The router began flooding other devices across the air traffic control network with connection attempts, disrupting both communications with aircraft and radar feeds.  A radar station in Amarillo, in the Texas panhandle, is also being eyed as contributing to the outage.   
And new flight cancellations reported for Monday already stood at 144 as of Sunday afternoon, with 641 delayed, reports ABC News (citing data from Flight Aware):
A spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop, said in a statement to ABC News that the devices were working properly Friday, when the ground stop occurred. "Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly," the statement said...
L3 Harris is a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers.  "We have that router in the L3 Harris lab down in Florida," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told co-anchor Martha Raddatz on ABC's "This Week" Sunday, referring to the specific router in Arkansas that officials believe caused instability in the air traffic communication system Friday afternoon.  
"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday.

articles.title: Siri Glitches Ruin Reviewer's Test of Apple's New 'HomeView' Smart Speaker
articles.body:
Siri Glitches Ruin Reviewer's Test of Apple's New 'HomeView' Smart Speaker (youtube.com) 26
			
		 	
				Apple has started selling its new HomeView smart speaker, a 7-inch square-with-rounded-corners screen equipped with a built-in camera.   It pairs with your iPhone or iPad to offer personalized content from your email or text messages, using facial recognition to identify each family member.
But in a video report, one Wall Street Journal reviewer discovered an issue while testing its smart home feature:
 WSJ REVIEWER: I've spent the last few years turning my home into a smart home that I can boss around with Siri. A smart lock, a special garage door opener, motorized shades, even a Raspberry Pi in my basement hooked up to my router that lets non-HomeKit devices from Ring and Nest work with Siri. It was all going well, the smart home controller of my dreams even.  But then...
Reviewer: Open the garage door.
Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app.
Reviewer: Siri, you have the Home app, and you're called the HomeView. Open the garage.
Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. 
Reviewer: Open the smart wifi garage.
Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app... 
WSJ REVIEWER:  Apple explained that for security reasons, Siri won't unlock your doors or open the garage through the HomeView using voice commands. You can only tap the screen to unlock them. The concern is that someone could shout a command from outside and gain access to your house. 
This security concern doesn't make much sense to me. This thing can recognize my face, confirm it's me, and pull up all sorts of information from my phone. But it can't recognize me enough to open my garage? Finally I got Siri itself to explain this top-security measure.
Siri: For security reasons, I can't unlock your door or open your garage from this device. Because anyone nearby can speak to a shared speaker.
Reviewer: But I'm looking at you!  You see my face, and you hear my voice!
Siri: I understand.  But I don't have a camera to see you. And voice recognition alone isn't secure enough for unlocking your home.
Reviewer: You don't have a camera?
Siri: That's right. This device doesn't have a camera, so I can't see you. I can only hear your voice, which is why I need you to use your iPhone or Apple Watch to unlock the door.
Reviewer: I see, Siri. You're gaslighting me. 
An Apple spokesperson said they'd send out a software update next month that would let HomeView unlock garage doors and other door locks by voice once it's recognized a user.  (And Apple said the update would also fix Siri's hallucination that it didn't already have a built-in camera.)
In the end, the speakers sounded good, and the reviewer appreciated how Apple's HomeView didn't have ads on its screeh like the Amazon Echo Show. But the device's built-in Siri voice assistant was "about as reliable as a Magic 8 Ball... And the frustration is so real. Sometimes Siri just doesn't get the voice recognition right... Oftentimes, other devices in the room think I'm talking to their Siri... And sometimes Siris just talk to each."
iPhone: Siri is built into your device, so you don't need to download...
HomeView: Downloading support for Siri.
iPhone:  To download the Apple Support app, open the App Store on your device, search for Apple Support, and tap get or the download icon. I've installed support.
Reviewer (muttering): I honestly could cry.  This might be a first —  crying.
iphone: I'm software, so I don't have feelings. But it sounds like you're going through a difficult moment. It can really help to talk to someone you trust, like a friend, family member, or a professional who can support you". 
They complained that sometimes Siri "is just slow, or it gets stuck thinking and thinking and thinking."  (It took three minutes to answer their young son's question "What's 10 times 40?")
They concluded HomeView's facial recognition feature works well, and so does its smart home functionality (especially when they fix its door-unlocking next month).  But its built-in Siri AI is "not great."  It's gotten better this year, and the reviewer found it "genuinely useful for some things on their iPhone.  "But Apple still has a Siri problem. And on a device that's supposed to be the intelligent center of your home, that's a big problem."
It reminded the reviewer of another new first-generation Apple product, the iPhone Duo:  "good hardware waiting for the software to catch up."

articles.title: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills, Reports ProPublica
articles.body:
Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills, Reports ProPublica (propublica.org) 51
			
		 	
				Environmental activist Bill Gates has "quietly accumulated a $29 billion stake in America's No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services," reports ProPublica, in a new 5,000-word investigation. But inspectors from America's Environmental Protection Agency "have repeatedly found methane — a highly potent greenhouse gas — escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits.  Republic has lobbied against regulations that could make the waste industry cleaner, including by keeping organic garbage out of landfills in the first place."
While Gates has invested at least $2 billion in green companies, he's "put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry," their article argues. And Gates has increased his stake in Republic "to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion."
While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They're responsible for as much as a fifth of the country's emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports....
[Gates] has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor... "It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic's behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits," said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder... Gates didn't respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn't find any public comments he's made about them.  
But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic's shares — "It's 'Garbage In' for Gates," the New York Post headline read — the company's stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows... A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune [in 1999]... To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he'd given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets... After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates' stake in Republic over the years that followed. [On behalf of the Gates Foundation] Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic's main competitor, Waste Management.
 
Methane emissions weren't a major focus of climate activism until years later
The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it's responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.

articles.title: Mini.nvim Is Now on Tangled
articles.body:
- Lua 100%
- Shell <1%
- Makefile <1%
- Scheme <1%
- Vim Script <1%
All-in-one plugin #
Library of 45+ independent Lua modules improving overall Neovim (version 0.10 and higher) experience with minimal effort. They all share same configuration approaches and general design principles.
Think about this project as "Swiss Army knife" among Neovim plugins: it has many different independent tools (modules) suitable for most common tasks. Each module can be used separately without any startup and usage overhead.
If you want to help this project grow but don't know where to start:
- Leave a star for 'mini.nvim' (on any supported code forge) and/or any other MINI projects.
- Check out contributing guides.
See change log for a history of changes, including current development version.
See MiniMax for a full config example based on 'mini.nvim'.
Note
This was previously hosted at echasnovski/mini.nvim. It was transferred to a dedicated organization to improve long term project stability. See more details here.
Table of contents #
Installation #
This project is hosted on several code forges (use preferred link in the installation code snippet):
- https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim (main)
- https://tangled.org/nvim-mini.org/mini.nvim (mirror)
- https://codeberg.org/nvim-mini/mini.nvim (mirror)
There are two branches to install from:
- main (default, recommended) will have latest development version of plugin. All changes since last stable release should be perceived as being in beta testing phase (meaning they already passed alpha-testing and are moderately settled).
- stable will be updated only upon releases with code tested during public beta-testing phase in main branch.
Here are code snippets for some common installation methods:
- (Recommended) With vim.pack (on Neovim 0.12 and newer): 
  - Main branch: vim.pack.add({ 'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim' })
  - Stable branch: vim.pack.add({
  { src = 'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = 'stable' },
})
- Manually with git clone (compatible with mini.deps):
-- Put this at the top of 'init.lua'
local path_package = vim.fn.stdpath('data') .. '/site'
local mini_path = path_package .. '/pack/deps/start/mini.nvim'
if not vim.uv.fs_stat(mini_path) then
  vim.cmd('echo "Installing `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
  local clone_cmd = {
    'git', 'clone', '--filter=blob:none',
    -- Uncomment next line to use 'stable' branch
    -- '--branch', 'stable',
    'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim', mini_path
  }
  vim.fn.system(clone_cmd)
  vim.cmd('packadd mini.nvim | helptags ALL')
  vim.cmd('echo "Installed `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
end
- With folke/lazy.nvim: 
  - Main branch: { 'nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = false },
  - Stable branch: { 'nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = '*' },
- Every module is also distributed as a standalone Git repository. Check out module's information for more details.
Important: don't forget to call module's setup() (if required) to enable its functionality.
Note: if you are on Windows, there might be problems with too long file paths (like error: unable to create file <some file name>: Filename too long). Try doing one of the following:
- Enable corresponding git global config value: git config --system core.longpaths true. Then try to reinstall.
- Install plugin in other place with shorter path.
Modules #
'mini.nvim' contains many modules which is slightly daunting at first. All of them can be used independently, one at a time.
For easier exploration, here they are presented in groups based on module's primary functionality (although some modules can fit in several groups). See more detailed listing here.
Text editing #
These modules improve your text editing experience. Start with 'mini.ai', 'mini.operators', and 'mini.surround'.
General workflow #
These modules improve your general workflow. Start with 'mini.bracketed', 'mini.files', and 'mini.pick'.
Appearance #
These modules improve your Neovim appearance. Start with 'mini.hues', 'mini.icons', and 'mini.statusline'.
Other #
These modules don't quite fit in any of the previous categories.
General principles #
Design #
Each module is designed to solve a particular problem targeting balance between feature-richness (handling as many edge-cases as possible) and simplicity of implementation/support. Granted, not all of them ended up with the same balance, but it is the goal nevertheless.
Independence #
Modules are independent of each other and can be run without external dependencies. Although some of them may need dependencies for full experience.
Structure #
Each module is a submodule for a placeholder "mini" module. So, for example, "surround" module should be referred to as "mini.surround". As later will be explained, this plugin can also be referred to as "MiniSurround".
Setup #
- Each module you want to use should be enabled separately with require(<name of module>).setup({}). Possibly replace {} with your config table or omit altogether to use defaults. You can supply only parts of config, the rest will be inferred from defaults.
- Call to module's setup() always creates a global Lua object with coherent camel-case name: require('mini.surround').setup() creates _G.MiniSurround. This allows for a simpler usage of plugin functionality: instead of require('mini.surround') use MiniSurround (or manually :lua MiniSurround.* in command line); available from v:lua like v:lua.MiniSurround. Considering this, "module" and "Lua object" names can be used interchangeably: 'mini.surround' and 'MiniSurround' will mean the same thing.
- Each supplied config table is stored in config field of global object. Like MiniSurround.config.
- Values of config which affect runtime activity can be changed on the fly to have effect. For example, MiniSurround.config.n_lines can be changed during runtime; but changing MiniSurround.config.mappings won't have any effect (as mappings are created once during setup()).
- If module works best with some specific non-default option value, it is set during setup(). If the value is not essential to module's functionality, it is done only if user or another plugin hasn't set it beforehand (no matter the value).
Buffer local configuration #
Each module can be additionally configured to use certain runtime config settings locally to buffer. See mini.nvim-buffer-local-config section in help file for more information.
Buffer names #
All module-related buffers are named according to the following format: mini<module-name>://<buffer-number>/<useful-info> (forward slashes are used on any platform; <useful-info> may be empty). This structure allows creating identifiable, reasonably unique, and useful buffer names. For example, 'mini.files' buffers are created per displayed directory/file with names like minifiles://10/path/to/displayed/directory.
Disabling #
Each module's core functionality can be disabled globally or locally to buffer. See "Disabling" section in module's help page for more details. See mini.nvim-disabling-recipes section in main help file for common recipes.
Silencing #
Each module providing non-error feedback (like a reminder to press a key after some idle time in 'mini.ai', 'mini.jump2d', 'mini.surround') can be configured to not do that by setting config.silent = true (either inside setup() call or on the fly).
Highlighting #
Appearance of module's output is controlled by certain set of highlight groups (see :h highlight-groups). By default they usually link to some semantically close built-in highlight group and are ensured to be defined after any color scheme takes effect. Use :highlight command or vim.api.nvim_set_hl() Lua function to customize highlighting. To see a more calibrated look, use 'mini.hues', 'mini.base16', or plugin's color scheme.
Stability #
Each module upon release is considered to be relatively stable: both in terms of setup and functionality. Any non-bugfix backward-incompatible change will be released gradually as much as possible.
Not filetype and language specific #
Including functionality which needs several filetype/language specific implementations is an explicit no-goal of this project. This is mostly due to the potential increase in maintenance to keep implementation up to date. However, any part which might need filetype/language specific tuning should be designed to allow it by letting user set proper buffer options and/or local configuration.
Text edit repeat #
All text edit mappings (like for operators, textobjects, motions) created by modules support built-in repeat functionality if technically possible. This includes dot-repeat, macros, and Neovim>=0.13 multicursor.
Plugin color schemes #
This plugin comes with several color schemes (all have both dark and light variants). Activate any of them as a regular colorscheme (like :colorscheme minischeme or vim.cmd.colorscheme('minischeme')).
- Based on 'mini.hues' (recommended): 
  - minischeme: blue and yellow main color scheme.
  - miniwinter: "icy winter" palette with azure background.
  - minispring: "blooming spring" palette with green background.
  - minisummer: "hot summer" palette with brown/yellow background.
  - miniautumn: "cooling autumn" palette with purple background.
  - randomhue: random background and foreground of the same hue with medium saturation.
You can see how they look in 'mini.hues' README.
- Based on 'mini.base16': 
  - minicyan: cyan and grey main colors with medium contrast and saturation palette.
  - miniblue: blue and yellow main colors with high contrast and saturation palette.
You can see how they look in 'mini.base16' README.
Planned modules #
This is the list of modules I currently intend to implement eventually (as my free time and dedication will allow), in alphabetical order:
- 'mini.abbrev' - helper to manage/setup Insert mode abbreviations.
- 'mini.cycle' - cycle through alternatives with pre-defined rules. Something like monaqa/dial.nvim and AndrewRadev/switch.vim
- 'mini.folds' - more capable and user-friendly folds.
- 'mini.repl' - extendable wrapper for REPLs with built-in support for R, Python, Julia, and maybe (just maybe) some AI tools.
- 'mini.sendtext' - send text between buffers. In particular between regular and built-in terminal buffers.
- 'mini.terminals' - coherently manage interactive terminal buffers. Something like kassio/neoterm. Might also incorporate functionality to asynchronously run code in shell with post-processed results.
- 'mini.quickfix' - more capable and user-friendly quickfix list. Possibly with preview and inline editing for search-and-replace workflow.
- 'mini.windows' - window manager. Interactive picker, layout organizer, and maybe more.

articles.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
articles.body:
All AI-generated code should be Open Source
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.
First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.
The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.
However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.
Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.
If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.

articles.title: Show HN: Gawain – Require type hints on all Python variables
articles.body:
gawain is a type annotation checker for Python. It requires annotations on variables, parameters, returns and class attributes, then runs a type checker, ty or pyrefly, to check that the types are correct.
Type checkers such as mypy, Pyright, ty and pyrefly infer the type of a variable that has no annotation. ruff's ANN
rules and flake8-annotations ask for annotations on functions only. gawain also asks for them on variables and
class attributes.
uv tool install "gawain[ty]"
gawain check src/
Warning
ty is in beta, and its diagnostics may change between versions. If that is a problem for your project, use
pyrefly, or --no-types to run the annotation checks only.
I built gawain only because I hate dict[str, Any] and wanted to do something about it. If your answer to
this is "but Python already infers that" or "but my IDE infers it for me", then don't use it, little padawan.
Given shop.py:
PORT = 8080
retries = 3
total = compute()
def send(to, body):
    print(f"to {to}: {body}")
class Order:
    def __init__(self, items: list[str]) -> None:
        self.items = items
gawain check shop.py prints:
[presence]
shop.py:1:1    GW001 variable 'PORT' has no type annotation
shop.py:3:1    GW001 variable 'total' has no type annotation
shop.py:6:5    GW003 function 'send' has no return type annotation
shop.py:6:10   GW002 parameter 'to' of function 'send' has no type annotation
shop.py:6:14   GW002 parameter 'body' of function 'send' has no type annotation
shop.py:12:14  GW004 attribute 'items' is not declared in the body of class 'Order'
6 errors (presence). Type check skipped until presence errors are fixed.
In the default mode, retries = 3 passes, because a literal has an obvious type. PORT is an UPPER_CASE name,
so gawain treats it as a constant, and a constant needs Final. The literal still gives the type, so
PORT: Final = 8080 passes.
When every annotation is in place, gawain runs the type checker on the same files and prints what it reports.
The default checker is ty. Given prices.py:
def total(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    return "0"
gawain check prices.py prints:
[types]
prices.py:2:12  ty[invalid-return-type] Return type does not match returned value: expected `int`, found `Literal["0"]`
1 error (types).
Install gawain with the extra of the type checker you want. ty is the default checker, and the ty extra pins
it to 0.0.100:
uv tool install "gawain[ty]"
# or
pip install "gawain[ty]"
To use pyrefly instead, install the pyrefly extra, which pins pyrefly 1.4.1 and does not install ty:
uv tool install "gawain[pyrefly]"
# or
pip install "gawain[pyrefly]"
Then choose it with checker = "pyrefly" in [tool.gawain], or with --checker pyrefly.
docs/configuration.md
explains the switch.
pip install gawain without an extra installs only the gawain command. It then needs a checker on PATH, or
--no-types to run the annotation checks only.
gawain check src/                  # annotations, then types
gawain check src/ --no-types       # annotations only
gawain check src/ --checker pyrefly  # pyrefly instead of ty
gawain check src/ --mode strict    # an annotation on every assignment
gawain check src/ --format json    # one JSON object, for tools
gawain exits with 0 when nothing is reported, 1 when it reports an error, and 2 on a usage error or
when the type checker cannot run. The type checker's warnings are printed but do not fail the check.
GW000 marks a file gawain cannot read, and GW900 and GW901 mark a broken or unused suppression. To silence a line, name the code:
value = load()  # gawain: ignore[GW001]
docs/rules.md has the full rules, the exemptions and the suppression syntax.
The default mode is obvious. A name may go without an annotation when its value has an obvious type and the
name is never assigned again: a literal (count = 0), a container of literals (ids = [1, 2, 3]) or a
constructor call (user = User("ada")). strict asks for an annotation on every assignment:
[tool.gawain]
mode = "strict"
docs/rules.md has the exact rules of each mode.
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/matheuzgomes/gawain
    rev: v0.3.1
    hooks:
      - id: gawain
pre-commit installs the hook from this repository's source, so building it needs Rust 1.97 or newer.
docs/configuration.md covers [tool.gawain], paths and the hook in detail.
On the CPython 3.14 standard library (1,847 files, 974,586 lines), median of 30 runs (5 for flake8-annotations):
gawain ran with --no-types. This is one benchmark on one machine (AMD Ryzen 7 3700X, WSL2).
docs/benchmarks.md has the versions and the commands to run it again.
- docs/rules.md: rules, modes, exemptions and suppression.
- docs/configuration.md: paths, output, exit codes, [tool.gawain] and pre-commit.
- docs/benchmarks.md: how the numbers above were measured.
- Issues: bugs and ideas.
gawain reads Python with ruff_python_parser and checks types with ty, both by Astral, or with pyrefly, by Meta.
I don't know, I just like the Arthurian tales. In Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Gawain repeats the Green Knight's covenant word for word, keeps every bargain he makes and slips only once: he hides the green girdle. gawain asks the same of your code: every type declared, and every declared type kept. The mascot is the Green Knight's axe with that girdle.
MIT. See LICENSE.

shop.py:6:5    GW003 function 'send' has no return type annotation
shop.py:6:10   GW002 parameter 'to' of function 'send' has no type annotation
shop.py:6:14   GW002 parameter 'body' of function 'send' has no type annotation
shop.py:12:14  GW004 attribute 'items' is not declared in the body of class 'Order'
6 errors (presence). Type check skipped until presence errors are fixed.
In the default mode, retries = 3 passes, because a literal has an obvious type. PORT is an UPPER_CASE name,
so gawain treats it as a constant, and a constant needs Final. The literal still gives the type, so
PORT: Final = 8080 passes.
When every annotation is in place, gawain runs the type checker on the same files and prints what it reports.
The default checker is ty. Given prices.py:
def total(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    return "0"
gawain check prices.py prints:
[types]
prices.py:2:12  ty[invalid-return-type] Return type does not match returned value: expected `int`, found `Literal["0"]`
1 error (types).
Install gawain with the extra of the type checker you want. ty is the default checker, and the ty extra pins
it to 0.0.100:
uv tool install "gawain[ty]"
# or
pip install "gawain[ty]"
To use pyrefly instead, install the pyrefly extra, which pins pyrefly 1.4.1 and does not install ty:
uv tool install "gawain[pyrefly]"
# or
pip install "gawain[pyrefly]"
Then choose it with checker = "pyrefly" in [tool.gawain], or with --checker pyrefly.
docs/configuration.md
explains the switch.
pip install gawain without an extra installs only the gawain command. It then needs a checker on PATH, or
--no-types to run the annotation checks only.
gawain check src/                  # annotations, then types
gawain check src/ --no-types       # annotations only
gawain check src/ --checker pyrefly  # pyrefly instead of ty
gawain check src/ --mode strict    # an annotation on every assignment
gawain check src/ --format json    # one JSON object, for tools
gawain exits with 0 when nothing is reported, 1 when it reports an error, and 2 on a usage error or
when the type checker cannot run. The type checker's warnings are printed but do not fail the check.
GW000 marks a file gawain cannot read, and GW900 and GW901 mark a broken or unused suppression. To silence a line, name the code:
value = load()  # gawain: ignore[GW001]
docs/rules.md has the full rules, the exemptions and the suppression syntax.
The default mode is obvious. A name may go without an annotation when its value has an obvious type and the
name is never assigned again: a literal (count = 0), a container of literals (ids = [1, 2, 3]) or a
constructor call (user = User("ada")). strict asks for an annotation on every assignment:
[tool.gawain]
mode = "strict"
docs/rules.md has the exact rules of each mode.
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/matheuzgomes/gawain
    rev: v0.3.1
    hooks:
      - id: gawain
pre-commit installs the hook from this repository's source, so building it needs Rust 1.97 or newer.
docs/configuration.md covers [tool.gawain], paths and the hook in detail.
On the CPython 3.14 standard library (1,847 files, 974,586 lines), median of 30 runs (5 for flake8-annotations):
gawain ran with --no-types. This is one benchmark on one machine (AMD Ryzen 7 3700X, WSL2).
docs/benchmarks.md has the versions and the commands to run it again.
- docs/rules.md: rules, modes, exemptions and suppression.
- docs/configuration.md: paths, output, exit codes, [tool.gawain] and pre-commit.
- docs/benchmarks.md: how the numbers above were measured.
- Issues: bugs and ideas.
gawain reads Python with ruff_python_parser and checks types with ty, both by Astral, or with pyrefly, by Meta.
I don't know, I just like the Arthurian tales. In Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Gawain repeats the Green Knight's covenant word for word, keeps every bargain he makes and slips only once: he hides the green girdle. gawain asks the same of your code: every type declared, and every declared type kept. The mascot is the Green Knight's axe with that girdle.

articles.title: Dffy: A fast terminal-native Git diff viewer, written in Rust
articles.body:
A terminal diff viewer for git, written in Rust.
Built for large repositories, up to the size of the Linux kernel.
dffy                   # everything you haven't committed
dffy main..HEAD        # any revision git understandsbrew install --cask amalucelli/tap/dffy
# or
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amalucelli/dffy/main/install.sh | sh
# plus the experimental Markdown renderer: … | sh -s -- --plugin markdown
docs/install.md covers mise, building from source and the renderer plugins. Then try it in any repository: dffy HEAD~10.
dffy is a diff viewer for the terminal. Run it in a git repository and it opens a full-screen view of your changes: a file tree on the left, the diff on the right, split or unified. Pipe it, and it prints the diff instead.
It's built for big diffs. Instead of computing the whole diff up front, dffy shows the first files as soon as it finds them and works on the rest in the background, so a 13,000-file change opens as fast as a one-line fix.
It fits into how you already work. Every action is a single key, the layout adapts from a wide monitor down to a phone over SSH, and dffy can stand in for git's pager, git add -p filter and difftool. Settings live in a plain config file you can keep with your dotfiles.
dffy builds on tools I like: the terminal review flow of lumen, the review UX of hunk, and the rendering of diffs.com (Pierre's @pierre/diffs). None of them fit how I work. lumen centers on AI features I didn't want in a diff viewer. hunk is TypeScript on a JavaScript runtime, and I wanted a single native binary that stays fast on huge repos. diffs.com runs in the browser. So I built a native terminal diff viewer that works the same on a laptop and over SSH from a phone.
Fast
- ⚡ Opens the Linux v6.0..v6.1 diff in 9.5ms and loads the rest in the background.
- 👀 --watch repaints as you edit, stage and commit.
Reading diffs
- 🪟 Split or unified, picked by terminal width.
- 🌈 Syntax highlighting for 18 languages, with changed words emphasized.
- 🌳 A syntax-aware diff (d) that marks reformatted (~) and moved (») code.
- 🔁 Renames detected the way git detects them.
Navigation
- 🗂️ A file tree, a fuzzy file picker and search across the diff.
- 🎯 Each file opens at its first change, and n/N jump between changes.
- ⌨️ Single-key actions, with a command panel on space.
Git
- 🧾 Staged, unstaged and untracked changes in one view, or any revision.
- 📟 Works as git's pager, git add -p filter and difftool.
- 📁 Compares files and folders outside a repository too.
Anywhere
- 📱 Works on phones over SSH, with plain-letter keys and a frameless layout.
- 🖱️ Mouse selection that copies over SSH.
- 🎨 16 themes and a config file for your dotfiles.
- 🧩 Renderer plugins (experimental), such as Markdown diffed as rendered text.
dffy                        # staged, unstaged and untracked changes
dffy --staged               # what's staged (git diff --cached)
dffy HEAD~3                 # a revision against the working tree
dffy main...feature         # changes since the merge base
dffy show HEAD              # a commit with its message
dffy main.. -- src/         # limited to paths
dffy a.txt b.txt            # two files or folders, no repository needed
dffy --watch                # refresh on every change
dffy --syntax v6.0 v6.1     # diff by syntax
dffy --stat main..          # also --name-only, --name-status, --exit-code
With git:
git config --global core.pager dffy
git config --global interactive.diffFilter "dffy --color-only"
In the viewer, n/N move between changes, f/F between files, / searches, o finds a file, space lists commands and q quits. ~/.config/dffy/config holds key = value lines; dffy config --default lists every key with its default.
🟡 means partial support; docs/benchmarks.md explains each one. All seven are open source. GNU diff is GPL-3.0-or-later and the rest are MIT. Checked against hunk 0.25.0, lumen 2.32.0, difftastic 0.72.0, delta 0.20.1, diff-so-fancy 1.4.14 and GNU diffutils 3.10; docs/benchmarks.md links the source for every cell.
Opening Linux v6.0..v6.1 (13,168 changed files, a 48MB patch) in a viewer, time until the first changed line is on screen:
As git's pager, dffy streams the whole 48MB patch in 3.0MB of its own memory, about as fast as plain git diff.
docs/benchmarks.md has the machine, the method, every command and the full results, including printed output against delta, diff-so-fancy and difftastic.
dffy is written in Rust. docs/architecture.md covers the crates, the data flow and the engine.
- 🧮 Its own diff engine: histogram and syntax-aware diffs, renames matching git's.
- 🖼️ Its own terminal renderer, with no TUI framework. A full frame takes about 200µs.
- 🌊 Streamed input and output, so the first screen doesn't wait for the whole diff.
- 🛰️ One shared watcher per repository, however many views are open.
docs/ covers every key, flag and setting: usage, the viewer, keys, configuration, themes, git integration, watch mode, renderer plugins, troubleshooting, architecture and benchmarks.
MIT

articles.title: Italy Fines Meta €805m Over Accessing Android Users' Photos with Facebook App
articles.body:
Italy Fines Meta €805m Over Accessing Android Users' Photos with Facebook App (bbc.com) 30
			
		 	
				The Associated Press reports:
Italy announced an €805 million ($887 million) fine against Meta on Saturday for using photos and videos from Android users' galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure...
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes. The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use.  
Italy has about 20 million Android users, notes the BBC, and this fine "is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant."
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts...  According to the Italian regulator, a preceding [authorization] notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery. The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".  It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation". 
"A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal..."

articles.title: Vulcan rocket fails during return-to-flight launch, 40 Amazon satellites lost
articles.body:
Vulcan Centaur rocket fails during return-to-flight launch, 40 Amazon satellites lost (video)
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites.
The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there.
"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today, 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."
Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket.
Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).
In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)
ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months..
"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.
That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it.
Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.
Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.
The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.
Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 15 with news of liftoff, then again at 1:45 p.m. ET with news of the anomaly and loss of the mission.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: Kiri – The Modern Container Runtime
articles.body:
New0.2.1 Mac · Windows · Linux
The modern container runtime.
8× faster than Docker.
Kiri runs Docker containers with one daemon. The docker CLI, Compose and the Docker API work as they do today.
The 8×: docker run takes 22 ms on Kiri and 178 ms on Docker Desktop (152 ms on Colima, 279 ms on OrbStack), every engine on 2 CPUs and 8 GB.
Free, and in beta on Mac, Windows and Linux. Something broken or annoying? Tell us with Feedback in Kiri's window, and we fix it.
Kiri's window is now in 15 languages
- 简体中文
- 繁體中文
- 日本語
- 한국어
- Deutsch
- Français
- Español
- Italiano
- Português (Brasil)
- Polski
- Русский
- Türkçe
- Bahasa Indonesia
- Tiếng Việt
- English
Works with what
you already use
- docker
- docker compose
- docker buildx
- Docker Engine API
- Docker Hub
- OCI images
- ghcr.io
- Dockerfiles
While it runs
Light while it runs.
Ten containers running on one Apple silicon Mac, one runtime at a time: how much CPU and memory each one holds.
CPU and memory · 10 containers running
Sample One Apple-silicon Mac, one runtime at a time. Measured numbers replace these soon. Benchmarks →
What's in it
Everything you'd reach for Docker Desktop for.
Containers were the start. Kiri now builds and scans images, runs Kubernetes and whole Linux machines, and puts any container on the internet with one click.
- Containers and Compose Every docker command you use, Compose projects grouped in the window, and a page for each container with live logs, a shell and its files.
- Images from Docker Hub Search Docker Hub from the window and watch each layer pull. amd64 images run through Rosetta.
- Builds, with a scan docker build through BuildKit, a Builds view of every build, and a vulnerability scan of each image on its own page.
- Kubernetes kiri k8s start gives you a k3s cluster in about 20 seconds, with Pods and Services in the window. kind runs too.
- Linux machines kiri machine create dev --distro ubuntu: your user, sudo, and your Mac folders at the same paths.
- Share A public link for any container on runkiri.cloud, from the window or kiri share web. More.
- Names and HTTPS Apps open at web.kiri.local, Compose services at api.myapp.kiri.local, with HTTPS from Kiri's own narrow certificate authority.
- Light on your Mac Unused memory goes back while it runs, and the VM sleeps after a minute idle. The daemon stays around 15 MB; waking takes 0.15 s.
- Move over in one go Bring your images, volumes and containers from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, then switch docker to Kiri from the window.
Prefer the terminal?
The commands you already type.
With Kiri open, the ordinary docker command runs on Kiri, and kiri adds what Docker doesn't have: a name for every container, Kubernetes, Linux machines and a public link.
- kiri run, kiri ps work like their docker twins.
- web.kiri.localhost reaches a container by name, no port to remember.
- kiri k8s start and kiri machine create for a cluster or a Linux box.
- kiri share web puts it on the internet.
Getting started
From download to a public link in four steps.
- Step 1 Install Open the disk image and drag Kiri to Applications. It sets up docker for you.
Download for Mac
- Step 2 Pull an image Search Docker Hub in Images and press Pull, or: docker pull nginx
- Step 3 Run a container Press Run and give it a port. It starts in milliseconds. docker run -p 80:80 nginx
- Step 4 Share Press Share on the container for a public link, or: kiri share 80
Compare
Same command, three routes.
OrbStack and Docker Desktop pass every container start through five programs, each with its own socket. Kiri passes it through one daemon that calls the kernel itself. Same docker command on all three.
Five hops. One shim process stays resident for every running container.
The same five hops, and a shim per running container.
One daemon creates namespaces, cgroups and mounts itself. Nothing per container is left running. Most of this time is the docker CLI starting up. Through the Docker API, a whole container lifecycle takes 3.1 ms.
Medians from one full run on one Apple Silicon Mac, every engine limited to 2 CPUs and 8 GB, all three through the same docker CLI with Docker's default bridge networking. Stops are drawn evenly; only the totals are figures. Windows has its own race.
Full benchmarks: p99s, the Docker API path and every raw figure
How it works
One small VM. One daemon. A socket between them.
On macOS, Kiri boots a single Linux VM through Apple's Virtualization.framework, with a custom kernel and a small Rust init as PID 1. The host and guest talk over vsock. Inside, the Kiri daemon creates each container with clone3. On Linux the same daemon runs on your own kernel with no VM at all, and on Windows it runs inside WSL2.
One VM, one daemonSee the numbers
Boot once
One VM serves every container. Cold boot to ready takes 112 ms, down from 810 ms on a stock kernel.
Talk directly
Requests cross one vsock channel into the VM, not a chain of Unix sockets. A round trip takes 31 µs.
Leave nothing behind
No process stays per container. OrbStack keeps a shim for each one: 143 running containers held 1.13 GB in shims on our test Mac.
Measured on one Apple Silicon Mac. Method and raw numbers are on the benchmarks page.
The app
A native app, not a web wrapper.
AppKit and the system WebKit on the Mac, Win32 and WebView2 on Windows, so no Electron and no bundled browser. Manage containers, images, volumes, networks and Compose projects, with live stats, logs, a terminal and files for each container. Running apps open by name at myapp.kiri.local. On the Mac it brings your images and volumes over from OrbStack or Docker Desktop, and lives in the menu bar.
Download
Kiri for Mac is out.
Every number on this page was measured on it. Kiri sets up a kiri docker context and brings its own docker, Compose and buildx, so there's nothing else to install. Coming from OrbStack or Docker Desktop? Kiri brings your images and volumes over.
Then, in a new terminal:
$ docker run --rm hello-world
Same docker and docker compose you use today.
